findings.why: The principle ... is real is a model opener, and genuine is an adverb-tic word that shows up four times across this short range. The last sentence of the paragraph (I haven't found this to be a useful cue) is Chris.
findings.verifier_reason: The principle that X is real opener and tell a different story is mild aphorism, and the paragraph closes on real Chris (I haven't found this to be a useful cue to look at in my career). Low on its own; kept because the whole T4 template clusters the same shape.

findings.quote: This claim does not appear in any peer-reviewed behavioral science literature. It originates primarily in a self-published 1999 book.
findings.where: Ch9, T4: Hair Part Direction, THE RESEARCH
findings.why: The literature and a self-published 1999 book with no title or author. If it is the Walters' hair part theory, name it; Chris hoards specifics, the model rounds them off.
findings.rewrite: There is no peer-reviewed study behind this. It comes from a 1999 self-published pamphlet by John and Catherine Walter, the True Mirror people, and nobody has tested it since.
findings.verifier_reason: Peer-reviewed literature and a self-published 1999 book with no author or title is exactly the vague-attribution shape. Note the reader's rewrite names John and Catherine Walter and True Mirror; that attribution is plausible but Chris must verify the names, year, and format before printing it.

findings.quote: Hair styling choices do carry social information — formality, cultural context, investment in appearance — but the directional claim is unsupported at any evidential level.
findings.where: Ch9, T4: Hair Part Direction, WHAT REMAINS VALID
findings.why: Paired em dashes bracketing a tricolon, then unsupported at any evidential level, which is the at-a-structural-level inflation move. The handedness aside that follows is the human part of the paragraph.
findings.rewrite: How someone styles their hair tells you something (how formal they are, where they come from, how much they care about how they look). Which side they part it on tells you nothing, except maybe which hand they use. Do not use it in front of anyone whose opinion of you matters.
findings.verifier_reason: Paired em dashes bracketing a formality-culture-investment tricolon, then unsupported at any evidential level. Chris never writes with dashes and the at-any-level inflation is the model's. The handedness aside and the do-not-use-it instruction after it are his.

findings.quote: Categories 01 and 02 are baseline reads: assess once, anchor early. Categories 03–06 are live reads: update continuously as the interaction moves. Build fluency in each category individually, then read all six simultaneously.
findings.why: Two mirrored colon-fragment sentences (assess once, anchor early / update continuously) followed by a symmetrical individually-then-simultaneously closer. Also carries the range's one en dash (03–06), which the standing no-dash rule covers.
findings.verifier_reason: Two mirrored colon-fragment sentences plus an individually-then-simultaneously symmetry closer, opened by an abstract-agent sentence (Eighty signals become usable). Also carries the range's one en dash. Pattern-y rather than unmistakable, so medium.

findings.quote: Appearance builds your background picture fast: socioeconomic range, occupation type, self-image investment. T1 indicators here are physical-evidence reads. High reliability when anchored to posture and social signals.
findings.why: Tricolon after the colon, then a subjectless fragment closer (High reliability when...). Every one of the six category blurbs ends this way; see chapter notes.
findings.verifier_reason: This is caption text under a radar graphic, so partly structural, but the wording is the tell: tricolon after the colon, a subjectless High reliability when fragment as the closer. Same shape as all six blurbs; this and 976 are the two worst.

findings.quote: Movement patterns reveal confidence, stress state, and social orientation. Foot direction is particularly reliable, feet orient toward genuine interest.
findings.why: Triple list plus genuine again. The comma splice at the end actually reads human; flagging mainly because it is one of six identical blurb shapes in a row.
findings.verifier_reason: Reveal confidence, stress state, and social orientation is just a plain three-item list of what the category covers, and the comma-splice sentence about feet reads like Chris dictating. No stacking inside the blurb itself. The six-blurb sameness is already documented in the chapter notes and by findings 9 and 12; this one adds noise.

findings.quote: A highly confident person can be entirely resistant to suggestion. A quiet person can be extraordinarily responsive. Always assess these separately.
findings.why: Mirrored pair (confident/resistant vs quiet/responsive) with stacked intensifiers entirely and extraordinarily, then an imperative one-liner. The caps NOT in the preceding sentence is Chris; the symmetry after it is not.
findings.rewrite: Confidence and suggestibility are NOT the same thing. I have had cocky guys who would not go under for anything and shy ones who dropped in ten seconds. Read them as two separate dials.
findings.verifier_reason: The caps NOT sentence is Chris. The mirrored pair after it, with entirely and extraordinarily as matched intensifiers, is the model balancing a see-saw. The Always assess these separately imperative is fine on its own; the symmetry in front of it is what a reader would notice.

findings.quote: Cognitive style determines which performance approaches land most effectively. Fast processors respond to rapid-fire reveals. Deliberate processors reward slow burns.
findings.why: Abstract noun as agent, then two perfectly symmetrical five-word aphorisms as a closer. This is the model's signature paragraph ending.
findings.rewrite: Watch how fast they answer. Fast thinkers love it when the reveals come quick. Slow, careful thinkers want you to take your time and build it, and they will resent you if you rush them.
findings.verifier_reason: Cognitive style determines is an abstract agent, then two five-word mirrored aphorisms (respond to rapid-fire reveals / reward slow burns). Reward slow burns is a phrase Chris would never say out loud on stage or in a text. Clearest model closer in the radar section.

findings.quote: Ten seconds. Five data points. One read. Run this in exactly this order, every time, on every volunteer, before you say a single word to them.
findings.why: Countdown triple fragment (ten, five, one) then every-time/every-volunteer anaphora. The direct instruction is Chris; the trailer-voice opener in front of it is the model.
findings.rewrite: You get about ten seconds. Look at five things, in this order, every time, before you say a word to them.
findings.verifier_reason: Ten seconds. Five data points. One read. is a countdown fragment triple, the trailer-voice opener. Chris's fan-blast register does hype but through caps and repetition (thank you thank you thank you), not through three noun fragments. The instruction after it is his.

findings.quote: Shoes are the most honest part of any outfit — they are the furthest from the face, the region most people actively manage.
findings.why: Reveal dash into an aphorism about honesty. The honesty framing then repeats at 986 (the face has learned to conceal) and 992 (honest summary), so the same rhetorical move closes three of five scan items.
findings.rewrite: Shoes are the one thing people forget to manage. Everyone works on their face. Almost nobody thinks about what their shoes are saying.
findings.verifier_reason: The shoes idea is a real cold-reading truism and Chris might well teach it, but the em dash reveal into an honesty aphorism is the model's delivery, and the honesty/concealment framing repeats at 986 and 992. One of these three is a line; three is a template.

findings.quote: Hands tell a story the face has learned to conceal.
findings.why: Pure aphorism formula, personified body parts, sits as a one-line paragraph closer. Reads like a pull quote generated to be a pull quote.
findings.rewrite: People manage their face. They forget about their hands. Calluses, bitten nails, a ring tan line with no ring: that stuff does not lie.
findings.verifier_reason: Pure aphorism formula with personified body parts, standing alone as the card's closer. Adds no information the Notice line did not already give. Reads like a pull quote drafted to be a pull quote.

findings.quote: The difference between a Supporter and a Challenger is often visible right here, before either has said a word.
findings.why: Third use of the before-a-word-is-spoken beat in twenty lines (980, 989, 998). One is a good line; three is the model reaching for the same button.
findings.verifier_reason: The sentence is fine in isolation and the Supporter/Challenger tie-in is useful. Flag stands only because before-a-word-is-spoken is hit at 980, 989, and 998 within twenty lines. Medium for stacking, not for the line itself.

findings.quote: Posture is the body's honest summary of everything else.
findings.why: X is the Y of Z aphorism formula straight from the taxonomy, and the second honest in the same list.
findings.rewrite: Posture rolls all of the above into one picture. If the shoes and hands say one thing and the posture says another, trust the posture.
findings.verifier_reason: X is the Y of Z formula, second honest in the same five-card list, and the sentence is not true in any checkable way. Textbook taxonomy aphorism.

findings.quote: High arm movement is one of the clearest indicators of elevated energy and openness. This is the number you are building the entire scan toward.
findings.why: One of the clearest indicators plus entire plus a this-is-what-it-was-all-for closer. Inflation, not information.
findings.rewrite: If their hands are up around chest height while they talk, you have found your reactor. This is the one you actually care about. Everything before it was setup.
findings.verifier_reason: One of the clearest indicators is stock inflation, entire is the intensifier tic, and the this-is-what-it-was-all-for closer is signposting. The Notice line above it (hands moving at chest height or above) is a concrete, usable Chris detail that the closer buries.

findings.quote: When you have three signals pointing in the same direction, you have a read. Commit before the moment passes. The performer who hesitates after a read turns certainty into a question.
findings.why: Three short declaratives escalating to a quotable closer (turns certainty into a question). First of three consecutive paragraphs (996, 998, 1000) that each end on an aphorism.
findings.rewrite: Three signals pointing the same way is a read. Go with it. The second you hesitate, the audience sees you guessing, and a guess is worth nothing on stage.
findings.verifier_reason: Three escalating declaratives ending on turns certainty into a question. First of four consecutive aphoristic closers (996, 998, 1000, 1007). A reader who knows Chris's stage voice would hear a narrator here, not him.

findings.quote: You run it while shaking a hand, while laughing at the MC's opener, while pretending to look for somewhere to stand. By the time you open your mouth, you already know. That is the whole point.
findings.why: While-while-while tricolon, then two punch sentences ending in That is the whole point, the exact that-is-the-whole-X closer from the brief. The concrete details (the MC's opener, looking for somewhere to stand) are real and worth keeping; the scaffolding around them is the model's.
findings.rewrite: Nobody sees you do this. You do it while you shake their hand, or while you are laughing at the MC's opener and pretending you cannot figure out where to stand. By the time you say anything you already know who they are.
findings.verifier_reason: While-while-while anaphora then two punch sentences ending on That is the whole point, which is the exact closer named in the brief. The concrete details (the MC's opener, pretending to look for somewhere to stand) are real and must be kept; the scaffolding is what needs rebuilding.

findings.quote: The read is never one signal. The read is the chain.
findings.where: Ch9, section closer after the ornament
findings.why: Never-X/is-Y contrast hammer with repeated subject, set off by a decorative ornament as the chapter's final word. Also reused verbatim as an epigraph at line 4718.
findings.rewrite: One signal is a guess. Three that agree is a read.
findings.verifier_reason: Never-X / is-Y contrast hammer with repeated subject, set off by an ornament as the chapter's last line, and confirmed reused verbatim as an epigraph at line 4718. Unmistakable.

findings.quote: "Eighty signals. Four tiers. One chain to read them all."
findings.where: Ch10 opener epigraph (falls inside this range)
findings.why: Countdown triple fragment ending on a Lord of the Rings riff. It is a pull quote, so semi-structural, but it is the fourth aphoristic closer in a row (996, 998, 1000, 1007) and the same shape as line 980.
findings.verifier_reason: Epigraph, so semi-structural, but the wording is the same countdown-fragment shape as line 980 and the Lord of the Rings riff is the fourth aphoristic closer in a row. Also worth noting for Chris: Eighty signals. Four tiers. is a Chapter 9 summary sitting as the Chapter 10 (Four Personalities) epigraph, so it may be misplaced as well as machine-y.

findings.quote: Territorial behavior reveals guardedness. Bag-contact + wall-seating + exit-scanning in combination points almost certainly to security, military, or law enforcement.
findings.why: Two triples stacked (three signals, three professions). The plus-sign notation reads like Chris's own shorthand and the claim is specific, so low; listing it because it shares the shape of the other five blurbs.
findings.verifier_reason: The plus-sign shorthand (Bag-contact + wall-seating + exit-scanning) reads like Chris's own notes, and security, military, or law enforcement is simply the set of professions the read points to, not a decorative triple. Specific, checkable, and short. Not a model tell.

findings.quote: In many cases, some of the most practically valuable behaviors are the ones whose research base is still incomplete, debated, or less formalized.
findings.where: Ch9, T4 Signals Removed intro, sentence before the sailor analogy
findings.why: Incomplete, debated, or less formalized is a padded triple, most practically valuable is inflation, and the sentence before it (Once again, that should not be taken to mean) is passive signposting. This is the model half of the paragraph the first reader half-flagged; the sailor line is the polished bit, this is the drafted bit.
findings.rewrite: Some of the most useful reads I have are ones nobody has bothered to study properly yet. That does not make them wrong. It makes them unstudied.

findings.quote: The predicted patterns did not appear consistently. Eye direction did not reliably predict memory access mode. The study's conclusion was direct: the NLP eye-movement model is not supported by available evidence.
findings.where: Ch9, T4: NLP Eye Movement Direction, THE RESEARCH
findings.why: Three short negative declaratives in a row, then a was-direct colon reveal. The citation itself is the best-sourced in the range; the delivery is a drumroll. Chris would say what the study found in one sentence and move on.
findings.rewrite: Wiseman and his team tested it three ways and the pattern just was not there. Where people look does not tell you what kind of memory they are pulling.

findings.quote: But under-eye wrinkle depth as a chronic worry read is not a defensible evidence-based claim.
findings.where: Ch9, T4: Deep Under-Eye Wrinkles, WHAT REMAINS VALID
findings.why: Defensible evidence-based claim is review-board vocabulary, not stage vocabulary, and it sits directly in front of the most authentic line in the section (I haven't found this to be a useful cue to look at in my career). The contrast between the two sentences is the whole problem in miniature.
findings.rewrite: Nobody has shown wrinkles track worry, and honestly I have never gotten anything out of looking at them.

findings.quote: High expressiveness signals an ideal reactor for any demonstration requiring visible emotional response.
findings.why: Abstract noun as agent (expressiveness signals) plus any demonstration requiring visible emotional response, a nominalized mouthful for what Chris would call a good reactor. Sixth of six blurbs to end on this shape; the reader listed it in notes but never quoted it.
findings.rewrite: If their face does everything their mouth does, that is your reactor. Put them in anything where the audience needs to see the reaction.

findings.quote: Eighty signals become usable when organized into six dimensions.
findings.where: Ch9, The Six-Category Radar intro, opening sentence
findings.why: Signals become usable when organized is the model's passive-agent opener; nobody is doing the organizing. It is the first sentence of the paragraph the reader flagged at index 8, so the whole paragraph is drafted, not just the mirrored middle.
findings.rewrite: Eighty signals is too many to hold in your head. I sort them into six buckets.

chapter_notes: Lines 771-930 are the back half of the 80-signal table (signals 49-80: signal, meaning, tier, category codes). Structural, not flagged. The meaning column leans on an X vs. Y formula (Comfort vs. self-protection, Politeness vs. genuine emotional carryover, Social dependence vs. independent processing) about eight times; fine in a table.

T4 Signals Removed (932-962) runs a rigid CLAIM / RESEARCH / WHAT REMAINS VALID template. The RESEARCH paragraphs are the most model-flavored part of the range: research consistently finds, meta-analyses find, Vrij and colleagues, the literature, a self-published 1999 book, all without a paper or title (the NLP section at 938 is the exception and names Wiseman et al. 2012 in PLOS ONE, which is how the others should read). The WHAT REMAINS VALID paragraphs each have one authentic Chris sentence bolted onto the end: I would certainly look for these when choosing a participant for hypnosis but I would not rely on this alone (947), I haven't found this to be a useful cue to look at in my career (955), Other than a possible indicator of handedness (962), I mentioned that earlier, but needed to state it again (932). Those tails are the real voice; everything above them reads drafted.

Coherence problem, not just cadence: line 947 (WHAT REMAINS VALID for smooth eyelids) asserts The wrinkle pattern encodes the person's dominant emotional baseline, and line 951 quotes that identical sentence as THE CLAIM being debunked in the next section. The eyelid section's valid paragraph is also actually about wrinkles, not eyelids. Chris needs to decide which he believes.

Broken promise at 932: the intro lists eight T4 signals as documented below (NLP eyes, eyelids, under-eye wrinkles, hair part, finger length ratios, ear shape, skull or face-shape reading, handwriting slant) but only four T4 entries exist in the range, and finger length, ear shape, skull shape, and handwriting slant appear nowhere else in the manuscript.

Six-Category Radar (965-978): all six category blurbs have the same shape: catalog line, one abstract-noun-as-agent sentence (Appearance builds, Movement patterns reveal, Territorial behavior reveals, Cognitive style determines, High expressiveness signals), then a mirrored aphorism or subjectless fragment closer. The pattern is 6 for 6. Quoted the three worst (968, 974, 976); 970, 972, 978 are the same move at lower volume.

10-Second Scan (979-998): every Tells you paragraph closes on an aphorism, and three of five are the same honesty/concealment idea (shoes most honest, hands tell a story the face conceals, posture the body's honest summary). The before-a-word-is-spoken beat appears three times in twenty lines (980, 989, 998). Then 996, 998, 1000 and the Ch10 epigraph at 1007 are four consecutive aphoristic closers, including That is the whole point and The read is never one signal. The read is the chain. This is the densest punch-stack in the range.
Adverb tics: genuine appears at 940, 955, 970, 988 (Curious or guarded? is fine) and 998 area; entirely/extraordinarily stacked at 974; entire at 995.

Dashes: 16 em dashes in the range, 12 of them in the numbered headings (01 — Appearance through 05 — ENERGY and AMTSCE — A MENTALIST...) and 4 in prose (953, 962 twice, 983), plus one en dash in 03–06 at 965. The standing no-dash rule covers the headings too, so the heading format needs a colon or period, not just the prose.

What reads authentically Chris in this range: the direct instructions (Run this in exactly this order; do not use it in any professional or performance context where credibility is a concern), the caps NOT at 974, the concrete staging detail at 998 (shaking a hand, laughing at the MC's opener, pretending to look for somewhere to stand), the hypnosis participant aside at 947, the handedness aside at 962, the plus-sign shorthand at 972, the clunky but honest I find it useful and I teach it as others will find it useful as well at 940, and I haven't found this to be a useful cue to look at in my career at 955. Keep those; rebuild the paragraphs around them.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model with Chris's notes stapled to the ends of paragraphs. The signal table (771-930) is structural and fine. The T4 removal section has a recognizable pattern: a drafted CLAIM / RESEARCH / VALID template with vague research attribution (consistently finds, meta-analyses find, the literature) and then one honest Chris sentence bolted onto each tail (I teach it, I would look for these when choosing a hypnosis participant, I haven't found this useful in my career, other than handedness). Those tails are the book's real voice and prove Chris was here; everything above them was not. The single most damaging habit is the aphoristic closer on every unit: from line 983 to 1007 every scan card, every radar blurb, and every paragraph ends on a quotable line (most honest part of any outfit, hands tell a story the face has learned to conceal, the body's honest summary, turns certainty into a question, that is the whole point, the read is the chain, one chain to read them all). Chris uses one punch per section; this section uses one per paragraph for twenty-five lines straight, and it flattens his actual instructional voice (run it in this order, hands at chest height, do not use it where credibility matters) into narration. Fix priority: strip the closers first, then name the studies in the T4 section, then resolve the line 947 vs 951 contradiction and the four T4 signals promised at 932 that never appear.

group.label: Ch10 DISC, Ch11 Volunteer Brain, Ch12 Tell Table

findings.quote: The most important application of DISC in performance is not the read itself. It is the adjustment.
findings.where: Ch10 The Four Personalities That Change How You Perform, section 'DISC and Volunteer Strategy'
findings.why: Textbook 'It is not X. It is Y.' opener, followed in the same paragraph by 'entirely different results'. Third neg-parallel in the chapter before any story or example has appeared.
findings.rewrite: The read is the easy part. Two performers can clock the same guy as a D and get totally different results, because only one of them actually changed how they opened.
findings.verifier_reason: Section opener is 'The most important X is not Y. It is Z.' followed by 'entirely different results'. No performer story, no example. Textbook model opener in a section that should have one.

findings.quote: The D-type is not just an audience member. They are an opinion-leader. Earn them early and they do part of the work for you.
findings.why: 'Not just X. They are Y.' straight into an aphoristic punch ending, right after two rule-of-three lists ('visible, they respond fast, and the room reads them'; I-types / S-types / C-types). Stacked model cadence.
findings.rewrite: The D at the table is your opinion leader. Get them on your side in the first minute and the rest of the group follows without you doing anything.
findings.verifier_reason: Paragraph opens Chris-like ('A practical note on sequence: win the D first') then stacks a tricolon, a 'not just X. They are Y.' and an aphoristic closer. The field observation is real; the last three sentences are the model finishing it.

findings.quote: DISC is a read you run on the way to something else. It is not a demonstration. It is a calibration.
findings.why: This is the 'Chris Michael's Take' box, the one place the chapter is supposed to sound like Chris, and it is the most model-shaped paragraph in the chapter: 'It is not X. It is Y.' then a colon-reveal closer. No first person, no venue, no story.
findings.rewrite: Here is how I actually use DISC: I never show it. Nobody in the audience knows I clocked them as a C/S in the first ten seconds and slowed down because of it. They just feel like the show was built for them. Which, at that point, it kind of was.
findings.verifier_reason: The one box labeled with Chris's name has zero first person, zero venue, and an 'It is not X. It is Y.' plus a colon reveal. This is the most damaging single paragraph in Ch10 precisely because of the label.

findings.quote: The value is not in the label. It is in the adjustment it produces in how you open, how you pace, and what you ask them to do.
findings.why: Second 'not X. It is Y.' in a four-sentence paragraph (the first is 'a communication style model, not a clinical personality diagnosis'), closed with a tricolon. Also a second 'on stage, across a table, or in the first thirty seconds' triple earlier in the same paragraph.
findings.rewrite: Nobody cares that you can label someone a D. What matters is what you do differently once you know. Different opener, different pace, different ask.
findings.verifier_reason: Second contrast construction in the chapter's first prose paragraph, capped with a tricolon. Pattern-y rather than unmistakable, but the reader's count holds.

findings.quote: For the D-type: precision is currency.
findings.why: 'X is currency' is a listed aphorism formula (taxonomy section 32). The S-type paragraph mirrors it with 'patience is the asset' and the C-type with 'logic must precede compliance', so the four paragraphs open on four matching slogans.
findings.rewrite: D-types pay you back for getting to the point.
findings.verifier_reason: 'X is currency' is a listed aphorism formula, and the four 'For the X-type' paragraphs all open on a matched slogan (currency / part of the story / the asset / must precede). The template is the tell more than any one line.

findings.quote: not just as a subject but as a collaborator
findings.why: Sits between the 1035 and 1040 neg-parallels, making it four contrast constructions on one page.
findings.verifier_reason: On its own a mild mid-sentence 'not just X but Y'. Kept only because it sits between 1035 and 1040, making four contrast constructions in eight lines. Downgraded from medium; it is a tic, the neighbors are the problem.

findings.quote: Eighty signals. Five filters. One practice.
findings.why: Numbered triple fragment stack as the chapter closer tagline. Every chapter in the range closes on a one-line slogan (1044, 1137), which is the model's chapter-ending habit, not a divider Chris would write.
findings.verifier_reason: Closing divider slogan in numbered-triple form. Not a heading, it is a manufactured tagline. Note the reader overclaims 'every chapter' closes this way: Ch12 has no closing slogan. Ch10 and Ch11 do.

findings.quote: he volunteer is not a prop. They are a co-author. And the most important casting decision in any show.
findings.why: Chapter drop-cap opener (the leading 'T' is on line 1057). 'Not X. They are Y. And Z.' with a sentence-initial 'And' fragment as the punch. Pure model rhythm in the first line the reader sees.
findings.where: Ch11 The Volunteer's Brain, opening line
findings.rewrite: Picking a volunteer is casting. Get it wrong and you are doing the trick for someone who is busy surviving being on stage.
findings.verifier_reason: First prose line of the chapter: 'not X. They are Y. And Z.' with a sentence-initial 'And' fragment as the punch. Unmistakable.

findings.quote: That moment — invisible, irreversible, immediately legible to everyone — is what this chapter is about preventing.
findings.why: Em-dash-bracketed tricolon of adjectives, sitting on top of a fragment stack ('Still technically cooperating.') and anaphora ('Nobody said anything. Nobody moved.'). Also 'precisely name' adverb inflation in the same paragraph. The whole 'What It Feels Like' paragraph is engineered staccato drama.
findings.rewrite: Nobody in the room could tell you the exact second it happened, but everyone felt it, and the show has not gotten it back. This chapter is about never letting that second arrive.
findings.verifier_reason: Em-dash-bracketed adjective tricolon on top of 'Still technically cooperating.' fragment and 'Nobody said anything. Nobody moved.' anaphora, plus 'precisely name'. The paragraph is staccato drama end to end. The em dashes also violate the standing rule.

findings.quote: Manage the volunteer's neurological state, and you manage the room's.
findings.why: Mirrored one-line punch closing a paragraph that already ends 'read this shift before they processed it consciously'. Second aphoristic closer in two paragraphs.
findings.rewrite: Keep the volunteer calm and the room stays with you. Lose them and the room goes with them.
findings.verifier_reason: Mirrored one-liner closing the second paragraph in a row that ends on a punch. Would pass alone; fails by stacking on 1060.

findings.quote: Most volunteer failures are selection failures. The right read in the wrong hands produces nothing. The right person amplifies everything.
findings.why: Three slogans in a row, the second and third a mirrored 'nothing / everything' pair, then the paragraph ends on a triple fragment ('a different strategy, a different set of signals, and a different set of effects'). Nothing concrete anywhere in it.
findings.rewrite: Most volunteer disasters were decided before the person stood up. You picked wrong.
findings.verifier_reason: Three consecutive slogans, the last two a nothing/everything mirror, then a 'different X, a different Y, and a different Z' tricolon. Zero concrete content in the paragraph.

findings.quote: The Supporter is your I-type: open, expressive, already oriented toward connection before you have said a word. The Performer is D or D/I: dominant, motion-forward, socially competitive.
findings.why: Seven triple-adjective bursts in one paragraph (Supporter, Performer, Challenger, Anxious/Reserved, plus the closing 'how to frame the invitation, how fast to move, and whether to lead'). The mapping itself is useful; the even three-beat cadence on every type is the tell.
findings.verifier_reason: Prose paragraph, not a card, and every type gets an even three-beat adjective burst plus a tricolon closer ('how to frame, how fast, whether to lead'). The mapping is useful; the metronome is the model.

findings.quote: Already leaning forward, already nodding, already sharing the experience with the people beside them.
findings.why: Anaphoric tricolon in the profile blurb, and the entry closes on two stacked punches ('Select immediately. This person does half the work for you.'). The signal list itself is structural and fine; the framing prose around it is model cadence.
findings.rewrite: They were leaning in and nodding before you opened your mouth, and they keep elbowing the person next to them.
findings.verifier_reason: 'Already... already... already...' anaphora in the profile framing sentence, and the card closes on two stacked punches. 'This person does half the work for you' is close to Chris; the anaphora before it is not.

findings.quote: Wants to be part of the show. Not as a participant but as a character.
findings.why: 'Not X but Y' fragment, then 'Will help you. Will also try to take the stage.' mirrored fragments, then the closer 'Give them a role, not a task.' which is copied verbatim from the D/I Blend entry at line 1031. The model restating its own slogan.

Two different intentions.', and 1154 as a standalone chiasmus 'Profiling reads the person. Reading reads the moment.'). Cut to one statement. The rule lines above the table (1157-1158) are the third appearance of the noise/read aphorism in the book. The closer (1162-1163) stacks 'decisions, not decorations' / 'That is the point.' / 'does not replace instinct. It builds it.' The one thing that reads like Chris: 'You will not use all of this at once. Nobody does.' (1163) and the observation that three or four signals become automatic after enough shows. Build the closer from that instead. Note the table body itself is a TELL_TABLE placeholder in this extraction, so table wording was not reviewed.

Cross-cutting: 16 em dashes in the range, 7 in headings (chapter titles and the D/I/S/C card headers, which are typographic and probably fine) and 9 in prose (1060 x2, 1078, 1113 x2, 1129, 1151, 1153 x2), all of them the reveal/aside dash. Standing rule says none should survive. Every chapter closes on a one-line divider slogan (1044 'Eighty signals. Five filters. One practice.', 1137 'Handle the person, not the trick.') and every chapter opens on a mirrored-aphorism epigraph (1051 'The volunteer chose you before you chose them.', 1144, 1171); that is a template, not a voice. Of the three, 'Handle the person, not the trick.' is the only one worth keeping. No contributor-attributed text appears in this range; everything is in the author's voice.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model that was handed Chris's outline, not like Chris. Of the 53 findings, 52 hold up against the text (every quote is verbatim; only 1094 is Chris's own stakes-and-clock opener and should be dropped), and I re-graded roughly a third of them down a notch because a single device in a section is his, while the stacking is not. The single most damaging habit is the negative-parallelism closer: 'This is not X. It is Y.' and 'no longer X. They are Y.' end paragraph after paragraph (1015, 1035, 1040, 1042, 1058, 1101, 1107, 1118, 1120, 1121, 1124, 1163, and more), and in 1118-1121 three consecutive paragraphs close on it. Because every paragraph ends on a reveal, nothing actually gets revealed, and the model then restates its own slogans to fill the gap (noise/read three times, timing-is-the-technique twice, who/what five times in twelve lines of Ch12, 'Trust it.' twice, 'Give them a role, not a task' twice). What is missing is the thing Chris's voice file says he does constantly: a name, a venue, a number, a line he actually said to a real volunteer. The Volunteer's Brain is his home turf and there is not one first-person show in it. The fix is not to sand down the contrasts; it is to replace each closing slogan with the story that would have made the point without one.

chapter_notes: Ch13 density: roughly 100 prose paragraphs, and about 48 of them end on a one-line aphoristic punch. That is nearly every other paragraph. Chris's real rhythm is one punch per section between long analytical stretches; here the punch is the default paragraph ending, especially from 1232 onward.

Negative parallelism ('not X. It is Y' / 'not because X but because Y' / 'the point is not X, the point is Y') runs about 40 times across 5,700 words, roughly once every 140 words. Worst stretch is 1245 to 1253 (six in nine lines) and 1284 to 1294 (seven in eleven lines).

Tricolons and triple fragment stacks: about 33. They cluster in the signal-catalog sections (Social Referencing Glance, Eyebrow Flash, Lip Compression) where the model pads each definition with a three-noun list.

Anaphora is the chapter's signature model move: 'It ties directly into...' x3 (1234), 'It helps with...' x5 (1276-1280), 'Sometimes...' x4 (1274), 'They may...' x3 (1298), 'If they press...' x3 (1301), 'It may be...' x5 (1305), 'X means nothing without...' x2 + 'X is useful because...' x2 (1308).

Near-zero contractions outside scripted dialogue. Every 'do not', 'it is', 'that is', 'I am' is spelled out for 5,700 words, which is the single biggest reason the chapter reads formal and machine-paced. Chris writes 'I'm', 'don't', 'that's' everywhere. The few places contractions appear (1229, 1240, 1243, 1244, 1303 'Please don't point this out... It's akin to revealing the secret') are exactly the places that sound like him.

Duplicated generations that should be merged, a sign the chapter was assembled from multiple AI passes: the unicorn/urchin paragraph appears twice (1231 and 1237); the NLP directional-map debunk appears three times (1186, 1190, 1247); 'You do not need the verbal yes / The body gave it to you first' appears at 1250 and 1266; the kids-glance-at-sibling social-map example appears at 1261 and 1268; 'The point is not to force one meaning onto it' appears at 1267 and 1274; the 'what the mouth is holding' list is regenerated at 1272, 1274, and 1305. Line 1236 also reappears verbatim at line 1989 elsewhere in the manuscript.

Vague attribution: 'Every study' (1186), 'The research that has tested that claim' (1247), 'Developmental research' (1261), 'Research on widened-eye expressions' (1265), 'Research in English-speaking populations' (1273). The T-tier tags are there but no author or year is named in prose.

Em dashes: 6 total (one in the chapter title, one at 1180, two at 1200, two at 1269). Low count for the chapter but every one is used as a reveal or bracketed aside, which is the model's use, and Chris's standing rule bans them.

Meta-commentary about the book as an object is a distinct tell here: 'I strongly feel it deserves to be in the book' (1275), 'Earlier in the book... are treated as' (1282), 'fits so naturally with the broader architecture of the book' (1284), 'Everything in this chapter connects back' (1307). Chris talks to the reader, not about the manuscript.

What reads authentically Chris and should be protected: the Fruit to Fang method walk-through (1216-1231, 1237-1244) with its specific words (apple, orange, elephant, iguana, unicorn, urchin), the scripted lines with contractions, 'I like the yellow ones best', the shoulder-shrug observation at 1237, the meandering pupil-response paragraph at 1257 ('One thing I have learned from experience... Just do not interpret the pupils in a vacuum'), 'It goes without saying that this works best on someone who is not deeply involved in the world of animals' (1238), 'stepped onto the wrong stone' (1289), 'that is gold. Start using this right away' (1291), and all of 1303 after the 'Not I caught you' fragment. The pattern for rewrite: keep the first-person method and the specifics, strip the aphoristic closers and the mirrored pairs around them.

Closing section (1306-1310) is the most model-shaped stretch in the chapter: summary announcement, four-line anaphora recap, 'None of these... All of them...', 'That is the discipline.', 'Not a catalog of tells, but...', 'The rest follows.' Every sentence is a device. Worth rewriting from scratch in Chris's voice or cutting to two sentences.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model that was handed Chris's Fruit to Fang method and asked to write a chapter around it. The method itself (1216 to 1231, 1237 to 1244) is unmistakably his: specific words, scripted lines with contractions, 'I like the yellow ones best', the shoulder shrug on 'Okay, I got one', 'stepped onto the wrong stone', 'that is gold. Start using this right away', and all of 1303. Everything wrapped around it is the model's register, and the tell is not vocabulary but the paragraph-closing slogan: roughly every other paragraph ends on a 'That is X.' or an 'It is not X. It is Y.' line, and from 1232 onward that becomes the default ending rather than the exception. That single habit, the manufactured punchline stacked paragraph after paragraph, is the most damaging thing here, because it flattens Chris's real rhythm (long analytical stretch, one punch, long again) into an even drumbeat of aphorisms that no one who has heard him on stage would attribute to him. Two things make it worse and both are cheap to fix: near-zero contractions across 5,700 words outside scripted dialogue, and six confirmed duplicate generations (1231/1237, 1250/1266, 1261/1268, 1267/1274, 1272/1274/1305, 1236/1989) that prove the chapter was assembled from multiple AI passes rather than written through. Of the 69 findings I dropped three (a heading, a legitimate causal 'not because' that also appears in the authentic pupil paragraph, and a punch line that is genuinely Chris's), downgraded four, and everything else holds on a fresh read. Recommended triage order: merge the duplicates, restore contractions everywhere, then rewrite the closing section (1307 to 1310) and the aphorism block (1232 to 1236) from scratch in his voice; the rest is stripping closers off paragraphs whose bodies are mostly fine.

findings.quote: You see the fear, so you soften.
findings.why: Lines 1428 to 1433: 'A better use is invisible.' then four 'You see the X, so you Y.' lines, then 'That is the mentalist's advantage.' Anaphora stack plus closer is the model's most recognizable set piece. The content is good; the delivery is generated.

findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 1429. Lines 1428 to 1433 are the full template: 'A better use is invisible.' then four 'You see the X, so you Y.' lines then 'That is the mentalist's advantage.' The advice is good and worth keeping; the anaphora stack is the delivery a model chooses.

findings.quote: Microexpressions are not there to make you sound clever. They are there to make your handling cleaner, your pacing better, and your revelations feel impossibly well-timed.
findings.why: 'Not there to X. They are there to Y' plus a closing tricolon, directly after the anaphora stack. Two textbook devices in consecutive paragraphs.
findings.rewrite: This is not about looking clever. It is about cleaner handling and revelations that land at exactly the right second.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'not there to X. They are there to Y' plus a closing tricolon, one paragraph after the anaphora stack. Two textbook devices back to back.

findings.quote: The reason this belongs in a book like this is not because microexpressions are fashionable. It is because they are one of the clearest examples of the book's central idea.
findings.why: 'Not because X. It is because Y.' as the opener of a section titled 'The deeper point,' which is itself a model closer habit (tie back to the book's thesis, then aphorize).
findings.rewrite: Here is why this chapter is in the book. Microexpressions are the cleanest example of the whole idea.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'not because X. It is because Y.' opening a section called 'The deeper point', which is itself the model's end-of-chapter tie-back move.

findings.quote: Wonder is built by noticing what the room has not noticed yet and shaping the experience around it.
findings.why: Thesis restated as a standalone pull-quote paragraph, abstract noun as agent. Fine once in the book; here it is the third one-line paragraph in a row.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Thesis restated as a one-line pull-quote paragraph with 'Wonder' as the agent of a passive. Acceptable once in the book; here it is one of four consecutive one-line paragraphs.

findings.rewrite: A microexpression is exactly that. It is tiny and fast and easy to miss, and if you catch it the whole performance gets sharper.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'Tiny. Fast. Easy to miss.' then a 'But if you catch it' turn. Manufactured staccato; nothing in Chris's corpus fragments like this.

findings.quote: Seven expressions. One-fifth of a second. That is the window.

findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Three-fragment coda ending 'That is the window.' Also the third different duration in the chapter (epigraph 'a fraction of a second', 1350 'half a second or less', here 'one-fifth of a second'); worth reconciling while rewriting.

findings.quote: Technical methods, systems, and practical frameworks. How the tools work at the level of mechanics, psychology, and application.
findings.why: Two rule-of-three lists in a two-sentence part blurb, verbless fragment then 'at the level of' inflation. Structural front matter, but the wording is entirely model.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Part divider blurb, so structural, but the reader sees it on its own page and the wording is entirely model: verbless tricolon, then a second tricolon after 'at the level of'. Keep as medium so it gets rewritten with the rest.

findings.quote: That lets you redirect before the audience hears the miss as a miss.

findings.where: Ch14, What microexpressions are actually good for (Second)

findings.quote: Some people are readable because they are expressive. Others are readable because they are trying very hard not to be.

findings.where: Ch14, What microexpressions are actually good for (Fifth)
findings.rewrite: Expressive people are easy to read. So are people working hard at a poker face, because the effort itself shows.

findings.quote: That is enough to begin. If the face moves briefly in one of those directions, you do not need to name the exact Action Units in the moment. You just need to know what family you may have seen

findings.where: Ch14, How to identify them in the real world, after the expression catalog
findings.rewrite: That list is plenty to start with. You will never name the Action Units live. All you need is the family, and whether it fit the moment.

findings.quote: The mouth may show contempt while the rest of the face stays socially neutral. The brows may flash sadness while the smile remains. These are common and easy to miss.

chapter_notes: Density is the story. Roughly 20 negative parallelisms in 3,000 words (one every 150 words) and about 18 paragraphs out of 61 that end on a one-line punch. Chris's real rhythm is long analytical paragraph, one punch, long again. This chapter punches almost every paragraph, often twice.

Negative parallelism ('not X. It is Y.' / 'You do not X. You Y.' / 'not because... but because') repeats ~20x. Worst stretches: 1363-1366 (three in two paragraphs), 1393-1397 (three consecutive paragraphs), 1434-1436 (back to back). Quoted the worst; the rest are the same shape.

Rule-of-three appears ~19x and is baked into the chapter's skeleton, not just its sentences: five uses, five variations, three zones, three moments, five training steps. Human chapters are lumpier than that.

Mirrored two-sentence punches recur as a signature: 'The audience hears the yes. You get the reaction before the yes.' (1359), 'The audience experiences fluency. You experience course correction.' (1412), 'One side is managed. The other is not.' (1393), 'The face was dressed for the occasion. The feet forgot there was one.' (1342).

Repeated generated phrasing: 'clean textbook version' at 1352 and 1378; the Matsumoto/Hwang subtle-expression claim at 1352 and again as vague 'Research suggests' at 1387; the chirality definition stated three ways in a row at 1393; the Convergence Rule at 1345 restated at 1347.

Em dashes: 14 total. Two are prose reveal dashes (1329); the other twelve are list-header dashes in the Leakage Hierarchy (1338-1341) and the expression catalog (1367-1373) plus the chapter title. Structural, but all still violate the no-dash standing rule and should become colons or periods before production.

The section 'The deeper point' (1435-1440) is the model's end-of-chapter template in full: tie back to the book's central idea, standalone aphorism, three-word fragment stack, then a three-fragment coda. Rewrite the whole section rather than sentence by sentence.

What reads authentically Chris and should be kept: the Ekman parenthetical '(who offers an excellent entry-level course that I recommend taking)' at 1332; the Dolly Parton 1977 Barbara Walters foot-kick detail at 1341; the mimic-the-face-and-feel-it tip at 1376; the heading 'do not use them like a carnival lie detector' and 'This is where performers get sloppy' at 1362-1363; 'shut up' at 1358; the concrete method applications at 1411-1415 (anagrams, psychological forces, dual reality, one-ahead) which are real craft even though their closers are model.

Signposting and inflation words are light compared to other chapters: 'This matters more than most people realize' (1378), 'entirely' (1363), 'explicitly' (1390, 1427), 'That distinction matters in performance' (1351). Vague attribution appears once (1387); the rest name Ekman, Matsumoto, Hwang, and Duchenne, which is good.

Small factual consistency flag for Chris while he is in here: the chapter gives three different durations for a microexpression (epigraph 'a fraction of a second', 1350 'half a second or less', coda 'one-fifth of a second'). Also 1336 has a grammar break ('consciously constructed, not because they are truly happy') and the 'left side is the honest side' hemispheric claim at 1394 is presented as settled anatomy when it is a contested finding; worth a hedge or a citation.
No contributor-attributed text in this range.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model with a good brief. The knowledge is Chris's (the Ekman course aside, the Dolly Parton foot-kick, the mimic-the-face tip, the anagram and one-ahead applications, 'shut up', 'carnival lie detector', 'where performers get sloppy'), but almost none of the sentences that carry it are: the chapter has no first-person field anecdote with a venue and a clock, no parenthetical joke past line 1332, and no long analytical paragraph that is allowed to end without a punch. The single most damaging habit is the negative-parallelism contrast hammer ('The goal is not X. The goal is Y.', 'You do not X. You Y.', 'not because X. It is because Y.'), which lands roughly twenty times in about 3,000 words and stacks three-deep at 1363 to 1366, 1393 to 1397, and 1434 to 1436. It matters more than the tricolons or the fragment stacks because it is what makes nearly every paragraph close on a pull quote; once those hammers are cut and the paragraphs are allowed to end on the concrete example instead of the aphorism, most of the medium findings dissolve on their own. The 'deeper point' section and the coda (1435 to 1440) should be rewritten as a unit rather than sentence by sentence, and the three inconsistent durations (a fraction of a second, half a second or less, one-fifth of a second) should be reconciled in the same pass.

group.label: Ch15 Closing the Barn Door

findings.quote: very performance creates an open question. What the audience does with that question is your last design decision.
findings.why: Chapter opens on a two-sentence epigram with an abstract noun ('design decision') as the landing. Chris opens with a hook line or a stat, not a manifesto sentence. Note the drop-cap E sits on line 1459.
findings.where: Ch15 Closing the Barn Door, opener
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. It is a chapter-opening epigram, and epigraphs are allowed to be aphoristic, but 'your last design decision' lands on an abstract noun and the next paragraph (Zach credit) is where Chris actually starts. Tic, not a crime.

findings.quote: Not hostile. Not cynical. Just a person thinking out loud.
findings.why: Two 'Not X' fragments then a 'Just Y' resolve is the model's staccato setup; it appears again at 1501 and 1585 in the same chapter.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Two 'Not X' fragments plus 'Just Y' resolve, and the same paragraph carries a second staccato run at its end, so this is stacking, not a single punch. The bar scene around it is good.

findings.quote: That is the danger. The impossible thing becomes a clever prop. The astonishment becomes a method guess. The room you built now has a ceiling. The barn door is open.
findings.why: Five one-line punches in a row to end the paragraph, two of them mirrored ('X becomes Y' twice) and two metaphors stacked (ceiling, barn door). The scene before it (bar, pen, nervous system) is good; the ending is engineered drama.
findings.rewrite: That's the danger. Ten seconds ago it was impossible. Now it's a clever pen, and the whole room just got a ceiling.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Five one-liners in a row with two mirrored 'X becomes Y' sentences and two metaphors stacked. Chris ends a story beat with one line, not five.

findings.quote: The effect is not just what they saw. It is the structure they build around what they think they saw. That is why this chapter matters. If you do not close the moment, they will close it for you.
findings.why: 'Not just X. It is Y' followed by a 'That is why this chapter matters' signpost and a chiastic closer. The closer is then repeated almost verbatim at 1582 and 1598.
findings.rewrite: What they saw is only half of it. The other half is the story they build around it afterward. If you don't close the moment, they will, and they'll pick the cheapest ending.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'Not just X. It is Y' plus 'That is why this chapter matters' signpost plus the refrain that recurs at 1582 and 1598. Three tells in four sentences.

findings.quote: That sounds simple. It is not. If you are doing the show right, you are subjecting them to novelty. New premises. New conditions. New objects. New assumptions. New impossibilities.
findings.why: 'That sounds simple. It is not.' is the rhetorical-setup move (repeated at 1475 'Those sound similar. They are not.'), followed by a five-fragment 'New X' anaphora.
findings.rewrite: Sounds easy. It isn't, because a good show is throwing new premises, new props, and new rules at them the whole time.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Setup-denial pair then five 'New X' fragments. The paragraph also opens with an 'In order for... In order to...' chain, so the whole paragraph is engineered.

findings.quote: They remember flashes. They remember feelings. They remember the gist. They do not always remember the architecture.
findings.why: Three anaphoric 'They remember' clauses resolved by a fourth negated one, with 'the architecture' as abstract-noun punch. Textbook rule-of-three-plus-twist.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Three anaphoric 'They remember' clauses with a negated fourth and 'the architecture' as the landing. Same paragraph as index 4, so a reader hits both in a row.

findings.quote: Not because the method was bad. Because the memory was loose. As the guide through the experience, your job is not merely to perform the method invisibly. Your job is to tell them what mattered. You are not just creating the event.
findings.why: Three negative parallelisms in four sentences ('Not because...Because', 'not merely...Your job is', 'not just...You are'), then a 'That is what closing the barn door is' punch. Densest contrast-hammer paragraph in the chapter.
findings.rewrite: The method was fine. The memory was loose. So performing the method cleanly is only part of the job. You also have to tell them what mattered, because you're building the memory of the event, not just the event.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Three contrast hammers in four sentences and a 'That is what closing the barn door is' closer. The densest single paragraph of the mold in the chapter.

findings.quote: Then something crucial happens. They agree.
findings.why: Announces significance before delivering it, using 'crucial' from the AI vocabulary list. Chris would just say what happens.
findings.rewrite: And then they agree.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Announces significance with 'crucial' before the two-word payoff. Chris would just write 'And then they agree.'

findings.quote: Now the audience is not merely hearing the conditions. They are affirming them. The participant becomes the witness for the prosecution and the defense at the same time. They certify the fairness. They certify the impossibility.
findings.why: 'Not merely X. They are Y' plus a 'They certify' anaphora, capped by 'That is the door closing' and 'the reveal has fewer exits.' The courtroom image is fine; the rhythm is the model's.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'Not merely X. They are Y' then 'They certify... They certify...' then 'That is the door closing.' The courtroom image is usable; the drumbeat is the model.

findings.quote: The reveal does not fail because they are skeptical. It fails because they solved a smaller, cheaper version of it.
findings.why: 'Does not fail because X. It fails because Y' is the exact contrast-hammer shape, and it follows two mirrored 'Instead of asking... they ask...' pairs in the same paragraph.
findings.rewrite: They aren't skeptical. They just solved an easier problem than the one you gave them.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Exact 'does not fail because X. It fails because Y' mold, and the same paragraph already has 'not just at the level of sightline, but at the level of meaning and memory.' Two hammers in one paragraph.

findings.quote: Memory is not a vault. It is active.
findings.why: Aphorism formula ('X is not a Y. It is Z'), and the same paragraph ends on a second one: 'You are not padding. You are editing.' Two contrast hammers in a four-sentence paragraph.
findings.rewrite: Memory isn't a recording that sits there. Every time you pull a moment back up, what's happening around it gets written in with it. That's why the recap matters. You're editing the file while it's open.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'X is not a Y. It is Z' aphorism opening a four-sentence paragraph that closes on a second hammer (index 11). Whole paragraph is slogans.

findings.quote: That is why the recap matters. You are not padding. You are editing.
findings.why: Signpost plus a two-beat 'not X. Y' closer. Reads as a slogan rather than a person explaining.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Signpost plus 'You are not padding. You are editing.' Same paragraph as 10; keeping both because a reviewer needs both grep targets to rewrite the paragraph.

findings.quote: Those sound similar. They are not. Negating methods is about closing routes. Impossible framing is about defining the mountain.
findings.why: Setup-then-denial ('sound similar. They are not.') repeated from 1466, followed by mirrored 'X is about Y' pair with abstract nouns as agents.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Setup-denial ('sound similar. They are not.') is a repeat of 1466, followed by mirrored 'X is about Y' pair with abstract agents. Pattern label 'rhetorical-qa' is loose but the finding holds.

findings.quote: You need both. You need to close the exits and raise the walls.
findings.why: Paragraph ends on a paired-metaphor slogan. One of roughly 58 punch endings in this range.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Paired-metaphor slogan closing the same paragraph as 12. The quoted audience thoughts between them are the useful part; the frame and closer are model.

findings.quote: There is a difference between a hit and a proof. A hit is correct. A proof is correct under conditions that make correctness impossible.
findings.why: Definition-by-mirrored-sentence. The whole three-line paragraph is a coined-term aphorism with no example or story attached.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. A definition is allowed, but 'A hit is correct. A proof is correct under conditions that make correctness impossible' is mirrored staccato with no example, standing as its own paragraph.

findings.quote: Each condition you add costs you almost nothing in the design. Each one closes an exit the skeptic would have used.
findings.why: 'Each... Each...' closer after a 'Fine. / Fine. / Fine.' triple. The skeptic call-and-response is actually a usable device, but the 'genuinely free selection' adverb and the paired closer are model finish.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. The 'Fine. / Fine. / Fine.' skeptic exchange is actually a decent device and could be Chris. Only the paired 'Each... Each...' closer and 'genuinely free selection' are tics.

findings.quote: Make them visible, make them unambiguous, make them real. Then land the hit inside the space those three conditions created. That is conviction engineering.
findings.why: Tricolon of imperatives, then a coined-term punch ('That is conviction engineering') that names the section heading. The model closes sections by restating the title as a slogan.
findings.rewrite: Keep it to three conditions, make sure everyone can see them, and put the hit right in the middle of them.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Tricolon of imperatives then the section heading restated as a slogan. Classic model section closer.

findings.quote: The content is the same. The conditions are different. Those conditions are the proof, and proof is a design task, not an afterthought.
findings.why: Mirrored short pair then a tailing negation ('not an afterthought'). Cadence is even and quotable; the preceding long sentence is the good part.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Mirrored short pair plus tailing 'not an afterthought' after a long sentence that is genuinely good. The closer is the only problem.

findings.quote: Distance is proof. Simultaneity is proof. Reverse revelation is the strongest proof of all. If you wrote it down before they thought of it, the timeline itself becomes the evidence.
findings.why: 'X is proof' four times in one paragraph (starting 'Speed is proof.'), abstract nouns as subjects, ending on 'the timeline itself becomes the evidence.' Pure staccato drama.
findings.rewrite: Speed kills the deduction theory before they can build it. Distance does the same thing. Doing it while they're still thinking does it too. And if you wrote it down before they even chose, the clock is the proof.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'X is proof' four times in one paragraph with abstract nouns as subjects. Unmistakable staccato drama.

findings.quote: The point is not to make every revelation fast. The point is to make the timing serve the proof.
findings.why: 'The point is not X. The point is Y' is the named pattern in the brief, preceded by a 'Sometimes... Sometimes...' anaphora in the same paragraph.
findings.rewrite: Not every reveal should be fast. Pick the speed that makes the conditions land hardest.

chapter_notes: Ch15 Closing the Barn Door: the dominant tell is the contrast hammer. Roughly 54 'not X. It is Y' / 'not X but Y' / 'Not because X. Because Y' constructions across ~105 prose paragraphs, i.e. one every other paragraph, with several paragraphs carrying three (1467, 1502, 1578, 1591). The 'Not because... Because...' mold appears verbatim twice (1467, 1502), and 'Your job is not X. Your job is Y' / 'The point is not X. The point is Y' / 'Your goal is not merely X. Your goal is Y' are the same skeleton with the noun swapped (1467, 1485, 1549, 1580).

Punch endings: about 58 of ~105 prose paragraphs end on a one-line aphorism, and thirteen of them start with 'That is' ('That is the danger', 'That is conviction engineering', 'That is the medium', 'That is enough', 'That is what profilers do'). Sections repeatedly close by restating their own heading as a slogan (1480 Conviction Engineering, 1547, 1594). Chris's voice profile allows one punch per section; this chapter averages one per paragraph.

Tricolons and fragment stacks: ~29 rule-of-three lists plus five-plus-item staccato runs at 1466 ('New premises. New conditions...'), 1501 (eight fragments), 1556 (eight beats), 1582 ('A line. A question. A confirmation. A pause. A reveal.'). Three anadiplosis chains land within four paragraphs of each other in Layering and Cancellation (1573, 1574, 1576): 'patterns are theories', 'theories collapse into wonder', 'fragments. Fragments do not satisfy'.

Repetition the model generated: the chapter refrain 'close the moment before they close it for you' appears at 1464, 1582, 1585 (variant), and 1598; 'courtroom brief' is used at both 1480 and 1566; the Anthem jump-scare shower-curtain passage is printed as his quote at 1494 and then re-rendered in staccato at 1556; Final Discipline (1582 to 1585) says 'one line, then reveal, then silence' three times in three paragraphs; the Key Principle box at 1596 restates 1591. Cutting the duplicates alone removes several high findings.

Em dashes: 10 in range (1 in the chapter heading at 1458, 2 in Kevin's script lines 1519/1521, 7 in body prose at 1550, 1552, 1575 x2, 1592, 1593 x2). All violate the standing no-dash rule; the body ones are reveal dashes and bracketed tricolons, the classic pairing.

Adverb and vocabulary tics: 'genuinely/genuine' 8x, 'entirely' 5x, 'deliberate' 3x, 'precisely' 2x, 'quietly' 1x, 'crucial' 1x (1470), 'the intersection of neuroscience and intuition' (1593), 'deeply human need' (1531), 'woven through' (1461). Signposts: 'That is why this chapter matters' (1464), 'Then something crucial happens' (1470), 'Here is the part that catches most performers off guard' (1533), 'That last one matters more than most performers realize' (1560), 'The real version is this' (1580).

What reads authentically Chris: the Zach Alexander credit (1461, 'Credit where it is due'); the Jamy Ian Swiss copper-silver story with the exact line (1498); 'Here is a post Anthem made on Facebook that explains this well' (1488); 'some of them are annoyingly good at it' (1532); the two hand-added sentences at the end of 1534 ('Just be aware of the frequency and believability of your miss. I also urge you not to always come out on top'); the Ice Cold / Morgan Strebler black Tesla aside with 'The fun part:' (1542); 'That last one is gold' (1562); 'Do not do that' (1560); the Rob Zabrecky reference and 'That said, there are exceptions' (1590); 'launder the prop work' (1575). These are the seams where Chris typed into a model draft, and they are noticeably looser and warmer than the surrounding prose. The Chris Michael's Take (1587-1588) has real specifics (Austin, forty minutes, the woman and her husband) but the cadence is fully model and should be rewritten first since it carries his name.

Contributor sections: Anthem's Facebook post (1490-1496) is the most human text in the range: caps, triple exclamation, ellipses, 'BAM, monster', 'I implore you to actually try saying some stuff like this'. Leave it alone. Kevin Hamdan's section (1507-1525) is mostly human (specific book and chapter citations, the K-letter script, 'We obviously know there isn't', four uses of 'powerful' with no synonym cycling) but the opener at 1507 and the closer at 1522 look polished into the formula; worth a check with Kevin.

The cold-reading principles list (1538-1545) is structurally a list, so mostly exempt, but every one of the eight items lands on a mirrored one-liner (horoscope vs reading, verbal fingerprints of a guess, Stay in the room). Consider letting two or three of them end on the example instead of the moral.
Lines 1599-1609 are Part Three / Ch16 front matter and infographic labels (T1T2, AM, SIGNAL CONFIDENCE TIERS); structural, not prose, except the epigraph at 1605 flagged above.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model with Chris's notes pasted in at the seams. The human moments are easy to spot because they are looser and warmer than everything around them (the Zach credit, the Jamy Ian Swiss copper-silver line, 'That last one is gold', the black Tesla aside, the two hand-typed sentences about miss frequency, 'That said, there are exceptions'), and they prove the point: Chris writes a long thought and then one plain line, while the surrounding prose lands a quotable on nearly every paragraph. The single most damaging habit is the contrast hammer, the 'not X. It is Y' / 'Not because X. Because Y' / 'Your job is not X. Your job is Y' mold, which appears roughly every other paragraph and often three times in one, because it converts every explanation into a slogan and flattens the rhythm that is actually his. Everything else (the tricolons, the anadiplosis chains in Layering and Cancellation, the eight-beat staccato runs, the ten em dashes, the 'genuinely' cluster) hangs off that same instinct to make each sentence close like a pull quote. The most urgent fix is not the worst paragraph but the one that carries his name: the Austin story in Chris Michael's Take has real bones and model cadence, and a reader who knows his stage voice will feel the substitution there first. Second priority is the duplicated material the model generated on its own (Anthem's shower curtain re-rendered at 1556, the refrain at 1464/1582/1585/1598, Final Discipline saying the same thing three times, the Key Principle box restating 1591); cutting the copies removes a dozen high findings without writing a word.
