chapter_notes: Ch16 Memory Distortion (lines 1610 to 1756, about 6,150 words, 111 prose paragraphs): the dominant tell is not vocabulary, it is the contrast hammer. I counted roughly 55 'not X. Y.' / 'not X but Y' / 'rather than' constructions, close to one per paragraph. In the applications section (1706 to 1749) almost every subsection opens with one and closes with a mirrored conditional.

Punch endings: about 52 of 111 paragraphs end on a one-line aphoristic closer, most in the 'That is X.' form ('That is the doorway into this chapter.' 'That is the ground under your feet.' 'That is enough.' 'That is the right question.' 'That is what gets repeated.' 'That is the story that should survive.' 'That is how a mentalist should use this.'). Roughly 15 'That is...' closers alone.

Repeated rhetorical moves that expose the template: (a) 'The audience does not need to X. They need to Y.' at 1718, 1731, 1738 with variants at 1715, 1723; (b) the mirrored conditional 'If X, the effect weakens. If Y, it grows/strengthens/lives' at 1711, 1716, 1731, 1740, 1747; (c) the pivot line 'That tells you when/how to use it.' at 1711, 1716, 1723, 1727, 1739; (d) three-fragment spectator-speak triples ('He never touched her. She named that freely. There was no way back.') at 1660, 1715, 1719, 1726, 1732, 1739, 1743.

Two paragraphs are generated twice. 1703 to 1705 (Chris Michael's Take: frame becomes high-status, audience watches the frame, whole thing weakens, strongest use is quiet, five-fragment list) is restated nearly verbatim at 1748 to 1749. And the 'science explains the machinery / performers show what is built on it' mirror at 1628 is reused at 1700. Chris should pick one home for each and cut the other.

The section labeled Chris Michael's Take (1701 to 1705) is the most model-shaped section in the chapter: a two-word opener, a five-noun-phrase fragment stack, and a one-line 'That is enough.' It should be the most personal section; right now it has no story, no venue, no number, no first person.

The Language Tools section (1674 to 1685) is seven consecutive paragraphs on the frame 'X matter(s) because...' (1679 to 1684) after three on 'X are useful/stronger because'. It reads like a filled-in outline. The content is good; the scaffolding should go.
Em dashes: only 3 in prose (1660, 1661, 1683) plus the chapter title at 1610. The dash habit was mostly scrubbed, but the reveal-dash rhythm survived as short mirrored sentences. Zero en dashes.

Vague attribution: 'serious interviewing doctrine' (1623), 'real work on memory updating after retrieval' (1649), 'established findings in memory science' (1655), 'the key-bending eyewitness material' (1693), the verbal overshadowing effect (1689) all go unnamed. Cognitive Interview (Fisher and Geiselman), Loftus, Wiseman and Greening 2005, Schooler and Engstler-Schooler 1990 would each fix one in a clause.

What reads authentically Chris and should stay: the propranolol / V2K / monarch programming aside at 1620 (weird and specific); 'This is a huge advantage.' at 1653; the rambling admission at 1655 ('as I am certain there is far more to learn than what I have laid out here. However, for a majority of our work...'); the hotel-pen example and 'I imagine you can think of more clever ones.' at 1659; 'This is especially important in PK touches or dual reality effects.' at 1658; 'It would be wise to even get a verbal agreement from the audience' at 1662; 'in case you are hungry to learn more' at 1665; the clunky-but-human sentences at 1695 and 1723. The book's own voice guide says 'stories have setting, stakes, and a clock', and there is not a single field anecdote in the chapter; adding two or three would do more than any line edit.

The posture interrupt at 1698 ('Notice your posture right now. Did you lean forward...') sits under the Performance Literature heading between 'It is worth placing the names cleanly' and the Derren Brown paragraph. Either it is a deliberate meta-reveal plant that should be moved to a section break, or it was generated in the wrong spot.
Tricolons: about 34 rule-of-three lists or triple fragments, heaviest in the Eight Mechanisms (1655 to 1663) where nearly every mechanism paragraph carries one, and in The Test (1752 to 1753).
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model from the epigraph to the coda, and the single most damaging habit is the contrast hammer: 'It is not X. It is Y.' and its sibling the mirrored conditional ('If X, the effect weakens. If Y, it grows') land close to once per paragraph, nine sections in the applications half open with one, and the chapter has no field anecdote, no venue, no number, and no first-person moment to break the rhythm, so even the section titled Chris Michael's Take is a five-fragment stack ending 'That is enough.' The ideas underneath are strong and specifically his (the eight mechanisms, the late clock, the sentence you want them saying tomorrow), and a handful of lines survive as unmistakably Chris (the propranolol and V2K aside, 'This is a huge advantage', the hotel pen, 'in case you are hungry to learn more', the broken 'garner' sentence). The fix is not line-by-line dash removal; it is one real story per section in his voice, cut every duplicated paragraph (1703 vs 1748, 1628 vs 1700, the 'does not need' and 'That tells you' templates), and then let one punch per section stand instead of five.

group.label: Ch17 Cold/Warm Reading

findings.quote: Not a compliment. Something specific — a pattern, a tendency, a private truth. Your talking stops. You feel two things simultaneously: the surprise of being known, and the weight of recognition that they are right. That combination is distinct from warmth or flattery. It is stranger.
findings.where: Ch17, WHAT IT FEELS LIKE (opening paragraph)
findings.why: Opening paragraph stacks a tailing-negation fragment, an em-dash reveal into a tricolon, an anaphoric pair (It is stranger. It is the experience...), and closes on two punch lines (That is the target state. Everything in this chapter is designed to produce it.). Every device in the brief in one paragraph.
findings.rewrite: Someone tells you something about yourself that you did not invite. Not a compliment, a pattern you thought nobody had noticed. You stop talking. You are surprised, and underneath the surprise is the sinking feeling that they are right. That is the state this whole chapter is built to produce.
findings.verifier_reason: Quote verified at 1772. Chapter opener stacks tailing negation, dash-reveal tricolon, It is / It is anaphora, and two punch closers (That is the target state. Everything in this chapter is designed to produce it.). Nothing in it sounds like Chris talking to a reader; it sounds like a model setting a mood.

findings.quote: Thin slicing, the Forer effect, context dependency, cluster reading — tested, replicated, documented in controlled research. When you use them, you are standing on solid ground.
findings.why: Em-dash reveal into a triple of past participles, then a one-line aphoristic closer. Classic model cadence; Chris's register would just say these have studies behind them.
findings.rewrite: Thin slicing, the Forer effect, context dependency, and cluster reading all have real peer-reviewed studies behind them. Use those and you are on solid ground.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1777. The dash-reveal into three bare past participles (tested, replicated, documented) followed by the solid-ground closer is a pure model move. Chris would just say these have real studies behind them.

findings.quote: This is not a performer's trick or a folk intuition. Emergency room nurses use it to triage patients whose charts say one thing while the body says another. Experienced trial lawyers use it to read juror reactions before deliberation begins.
findings.why: Negative opener, then three anaphoric professions (nurses, lawyers, hostage negotiators) with no source for any of them, then a tricolon summary and the punch That is thin slicing. Unsourced professional examples in a triple are a model habit.
findings.rewrite: Performers are not the only people doing this. ER nurses triage on it when the chart says one thing and the patient's body says another. Trial lawyers read jurors with it. In every case the judgment is fast, comes from a tiny sample, and beats chance by a margin you can measure.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1780. Negative opener, three unsourced professions in identical sentence shape, a tricolon summary, then That is thin slicing. The professions are plausible but nobody is named, which is the vague-authority tell on top of the cadence.

findings.quote: Do not prescribe. You are reading behavior. You are not directing lives. Never tell someone what to do, what their relationship means, or what their future holds. State what you see. Frame it as insight, not instruction.
findings.where: Ch17, The Four Principles of Translation, 04 Observe
findings.why: Six clipped imperatives and negations in a row, a tricolon, an insight-not-instruction contrast, then a punch ending about real consequences. The heading is fine; the body is pure staccato drama.
findings.rewrite: You are reading behavior, not running someone's life. Never tell a participant what to do, what their relationship means, or where their future is headed. Say what you see and stop there. Once you start giving advice you are not performing anymore, and the consequences are real.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1822. Downgraded from high: this is a numbered instruction block and Chris does give direct orders. What is still model is the You are reading behavior / You are not directing lives contrast, the insight-not-instruction tail, and the ominous closer. Note all four principles (1813, 1816, 1819, 1822) end on an aphoristic closer, which is the density problem.

findings.quote: The room matters. The event matters. The age of the participant matters. Their relationship to the people around them matters. The way they hold themselves while waiting matters. Even silence is not empty. Silence is behavior, and it is readable.
findings.why: Five consecutive sentences ending in matters, followed by a negation and an aphoristic closer. Unmistakable model rhythm.
findings.rewrite: A reading never starts at zero. The room, the event, how old they are, who they came with, how they stand while they wait for you to get to them: all of that is information before you say a word. Even silence tells you something.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1824. Five consecutive sentences ending in matters, then Even silence is not empty. Silence is behavior, and it is readable. Unmistakable.

findings.quote: The skill is not in noticing a single cue. The skill is in interpreting cues inside a living frame.
findings.why: The skill is not X. The skill is Y. as a paragraph closer, directly after the anaphora paragraph. Also carries genuine certainty as a filler adjective.
findings.rewrite: Noticing one cue is easy. The skill is reading that cue against everything else going on around it.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1825. The skill is not X. The skill is Y. as a closer, immediately after the anaphora paragraph, plus the mirrored ring/answer pair and genuine as filler. Two paragraphs in a row closing on a formula.

findings.quote: A stock line says: I know a type. A strong reading says: I notice you. That difference is everything. People do not remember readings because the performer accumulated hits. They remember them because the reading felt specific, personal, and emotionally true.
findings.where: Ch17, Stock Lines vs. Seeing the Person
findings.why: Mirrored aphorism pair, That difference is everything punch, a not-because/because parallel, then a closing tricolon. Four devices in five sentences.
findings.rewrite: A stock line tells someone what type they are. A good read tells them you noticed them specifically. Nobody remembers how many hits you got. They remember the one line that felt like it was written for them.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1830. Mirrored says/says pair, That difference is everything, not-because/because, closing tricolon. Note A strong reading says: I notice you is also the deck pull-quote at 1770, so this paragraph is what the chapter chose to advertise; it needs Chris's own words most.

findings.quote: If your tone communicates 'I am analyzing you,' the participant becomes guarded. If it communicates 'I am noticing something human and real here,' the same insight lands with far more force. That is the difference between dissection and recognition.
findings.why: This box is literally labeled as Chris's own take and it reads the most model of anything nearby: matched If/If sentences and a That is the difference between X and Y closer. Highest priority to rewrite in his actual voice.
findings.rewrite: The fastest way to kill a reading is to sound clinical. If the participant feels analyzed, they close up. If they feel noticed, the exact same sentence lands twice as hard.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1832. The box is labeled as Chris's own take and reads the most machine-made in the section: matched If/If sentences and That is the difference between dissection and recognition. Top priority for a hand rewrite.

findings.quote: published research that quietly redrew the boundary between intuition and science.
findings.why: quietly as an inflation adverb plus redrew the boundary between intuition and science is significance puffing (taxonomy section 1). The study is real; the ceremony is the model's.
findings.rewrite: In 1992 Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal published a study that moved the line between gut feeling and science.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1834. quietly redrew the boundary between intuition and science is taxonomy section 1 significance puffing with the quietly adverb. The study is real; the ceremony is not Chris.

findings.quote: Not a full interview or a battery of assessments — just seconds of observation, sometimes less.
findings.why: Not X — just Y reveal dash with a tailing fragment. Same move repeats on the next line (no audio and no context — just behavior).
findings.rewrite: No interview, no test battery. A few seconds of watching someone, sometimes less.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1834. Not X — just Y reveal dash with a sometimes less tail, and the same move repeats on 1835 (no audio and no context — just behavior). Same paragraph as index 8 but a separate fix.

findings.quote: produces better rapport, faster trust, and stronger compliance. Use the framework I am about to give you. Know what it is and what it is not.

The paragraph also opens with To be precise about the evidence base: signposting. The imperative pair could be Chris; the whole paragraph around it is not.

findings.quote: the underlying mechanistic claims have not been robustly confirmed. What has been confirmed, repeatedly, in high-stakes practitioner settings

findings.rewrite: nobody has proven the mechanism behind it. What does hold up, in interrogation rooms and on stage, is

findings.quote: Something shifted in his expression. Not surprise. Recognition. You continue: People lean on you more than they should. You rarely name that directly. He set down his drink. The read had traction. You let it land.
findings.where: Ch17, Cold Reading in Practice, Close-up context
findings.why: Not surprise. Recognition. is the exact fragment pattern in the brief, followed by four clipped sentences and the You let it land closer. The vignette is also nameless and venue-less, unlike Chris's real anecdotes.
findings.rewrite: His face changed, and it was not surprise, he recognized it. You keep going: people lean on you more than they should, and you almost never say so out loud. He set his drink down. That is your cue to shut up and let it sit.

findings.quote: The association was built through proximity, not argument. Words that appear near each other become associated. The association becomes belief. The belief becomes invisible.
findings.why: Tailing negation then a climbing chain (associated, association, belief, belief, invisible) ending in a one-line aphorism. Also Baker and his associates is a vague citation for a real, nameable 2008 study.
findings.rewrite: The press was linking those four words in readers' minds whether the individual writers meant to or not. Nobody argued the connection. It got built by putting the words next to each other, over and over, until readers stopped noticing it was there.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1886. Tailing not argument, then an anadiplosis chain (associated, association, belief, belief, invisible). Also Baker and his associates is a nameable study (Paul Baker et al., 2008, Discourse and Society) left vague.

findings.quote: The words they place near each other reveal their private architecture of meaning: which concepts live together in their mind, which ideas are emotionally fused, which associations they carry without knowing they carry them.
findings.why: Anaphoric which/which/which tricolon after the architecture of aphorism formula (taxonomy section 32), opened by a This matters because signpost.
findings.rewrite: Nobody picks words at random. The words someone keeps putting next to each other show you which ideas are wired together in their head, including the ones they do not know are connected.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1887. This matters because signpost, private architecture of meaning aphorism formula, then a which/which/which tricolon.

findings.quote: Both will respond to being read accurately. Neither will expect you to have seen the distinction. The read lands because you are naming something that exists below their conscious self-presentation.
findings.where: Ch17, Collocation as a Pre-Show Tool
findings.why: Two mirrored CEO sentences, then Both/Neither antithesis, then an abstract closer (below their conscious self-presentation). Whole paragraph is built on symmetry.
findings.rewrite: A CEO who keeps putting team next to push and performance treats the team as a tool. One who puts team next to trust and together treats it as a relationship. Read either one accurately and it lands, because neither of them expects you to have spotted that from an email.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1898. Downgraded: the two CEO sentences are a legitimate teaching contrast. What reads model is the Both/Neither antithesis and the below their conscious self-presentation closer. Fix the last two sentences, keep the example.

findings.quote: People manage what they say. They do not manage which words they place near each other. Content is curated. Proximity is automatic.
findings.where: Ch17, Why Collocation Works Where Direct Statements Fail
findings.why: Three stacked contrast pairs in one paragraph (manage/do not manage, curated/automatic, can rehearse/cannot rehearse) closing on the tailing-negation aphorism The signal is in the structure, not the story.
findings.rewrite: People control what they say. They do not control which words end up next to each other. You can rehearse your answer to tell me about yourself. You cannot rehearse the word pairings that show up over the next five unguarded minutes.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1900. Three stacked contrast pairs in one paragraph ending on The signal is in the structure, not the story. This paragraph is the contrast hammer at full swing.

findings.quote: It is not a guess that happens to fit. It is an observation about how they think, rendered visible through how they speak.
findings.where: Ch17, Why Collocation Works Where Direct Statements Fail
findings.why: It is not X. It is Y. plus a chiastic how they think / how they speak closer, right after a mirrored Barnum-statement / collocation-read pair. Second symmetric paragraph in a row.
findings.rewrite: That is why a collocation read feels different. A Barnum line is true of most people. A collocation read is true of the way this one person files their experience, and they can feel the difference.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1901. It is not X. It is Y. plus the how they think / how they speak chiasmus, directly after the mirrored Barnum/collocation pair. Second symmetric paragraph in a row.

findings.quote: Cold reading is not guessing. It is observing, reflecting, and delivering in a register that the person cannot dismiss. The Forer effect does not make a cold read land. Delivery does. Specificity does. The emotional register you bring to the room does.
findings.where: Ch17, IF YOU REMEMBER NOTHING ELSE
findings.why: Two negative parallelisms, a tricolon of gerunds, and a does/does/does anaphora with abstract nouns as agents, all in four lines. Opens the densest cluster in the range.
findings.rewrite: Cold reading is observation delivered with enough confidence that the person cannot wave it off. The Forer effect gets you in the door. How you deliver it decides whether it lands.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1903. Two negative parallelisms, a gerund tricolon, and does/does/does with abstract nouns as agents. Opens the densest cluster in the range.

findings.quote: Collocation is not a technique you announce. It is something you hear. The content is managed. The proximity is not. If you are listening at that level, you are operating on a different floor from most readers in the room.
findings.where: Ch17, IF YOU REMEMBER NOTHING ELSE
findings.why: Third consecutive summary paragraph built on is not X / It is Y, with a second contrast pair and a different-floor aphorism closer.
findings.rewrite: You never announce collocation. You just listen for it. If you are hearing at that level you are ahead of almost every reader in the room.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1905. Third consecutive summary paragraph on the is-not/It-is frame with a different-floor aphorism closer.

findings.quote: And a psychological force is not about steering someone against their will. It is about making one answer easier than all the others. When it works, they feel like they arrived there themselves. That is the point.
findings.where: Ch17, IF YOU REMEMBER NOTHING ELSE
findings.why: is not about X. It is about Y. plus That is the point. closer. Also psychological force is never discussed anywhere in this chapter, so the summary line looks pasted in from another chapter's draft.
findings.rewrite: A psychological force does not push someone against their will. It makes one answer a little easier to reach than the others, so when they pick it, it feels like their own idea.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1906. is not about X. It is about Y. plus That is the point. The observation that psychological force never appears anywhere else in this chapter is correct; this paragraph belongs to some other chapter's summary.

findings.quote: The mechanism disappears. The perception remains.
findings.where: Ch17, IF YOU REMEMBER NOTHING ELSE (final line before the epigraph)
findings.why: Free-floating mirrored aphorism as chapter closer, immediately followed by a second aphorism at 1909. Two quotable closers in a row is the model, not Chris.
findings.rewrite: Cut. Let 1909 carry the close on its own.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1907. Free-floating mirrored aphorism immediately followed by a second closer at 1909. Two quotables in a row is the model; cut this one and let 1909 close.

findings.quote: His readings are not just technically precise but are precise in the way that only comes from someone who has thought carefully about why they work, not just how.
findings.where: Ch17, A Note on Two People Referenced in This Chapter
findings.why: Doubled not just in one sentence. The rest of the paragraph (APCA 2025 and 2026, three hundred shows in twenty countries) is authentic Chris specificity; this sentence is the model padding around it.
findings.rewrite: His readings are technically precise, and more than that, he has actually thought about why they work, not just how.

findings.quote: The clips contained no words, no content, and no context. The accuracy came entirely from behavioral pattern.

findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1784. not X, it is Y with entire as inflation inside a glossary entry. One representative of roughly a dozen is-not/It-is pairs in the range.

findings.quote: You are not fabricating insight. You are surfacing what was already there and handing it back with confidence.
findings.where: Ch17, IF YOU REMEMBER NOTHING ELSE
findings.why: Second of five consecutive summary paragraphs built on the same You are not X / You are Y frame.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1904. You are not X. You are Y. as the second of five summary paragraphs on the same frame. Medium on its own; the neighbors carry the highs.

findings.quote: The best cold read is a warm observation delivered cold.
findings.why: Chiastic aphorism as sign-off. On its own a closing line is Chris's habit; stacked right after The mechanism disappears. The perception remains. it reads as the model producing two quotables for the price of one. Keep this one, cut 1907.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1909. Downgraded: a single chiastic sign-off is Chris's habit and this is the earned closer of the chapter. It only reads model because 1907 sits right in front of it. Keep this line, cut 1907.

findings.quote: COLD READING, WARM READING, AND THIN SLICING
findings.where: Ch17 chapter heading (CHAPTER 17 — ...); the dash is wrapped in non-breaking spaces
findings.why: Structural, but the heading carries an em dash and the standing rule is no em dashes anywhere public.
findings.verifier_reason: Chapter heading. Structural per the brief; the em dash is a typographic template issue for the no-dash production sweep, not a voice or cadence finding.

findings.quote: Here is the science, the craft, and the honest account of what each is.
findings.where: Ch17 deck line under the heading
findings.why: Rule-of-three deck line and it is the first sentence of the chapter, so it sets the model rhythm before the prose starts.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1770. Deck line under the heading. One tricolon is not a tell, but the honest account of what each is has the model's hedge flavor and it is the first sentence the reader sees, so it sets the rhythm.

findings.quote: Widely used by performers and intelligence professionals.
findings.why: Subjectless fragment with unnamed authorities; one of a cluster of unsourced credibility claims (1780, 1789, 1835, 1838).
findings.verifier_reason: Verified at 1789. Subjectless fragment with unnamed authorities. Low alone, but it is one of a cluster of five unsourced credibility claims (1780, 1787, 1789, 1791, 1835, 1838), which together read like a model filling a citation gap.

findings.quote: You already know more than you think. The trick is knowing what to trust.
findings.where: Ch18 opening epigraph (inside the audited range but belongs to Chapter 18)
findings.why: Two-beat quotable epigraph in the same formula as the Ch17 closers. Unattributed, so it reads as generated.
findings.verifier_reason: Chapter 18 epigraph, a quoted structural element outside Chapter 17. A single two-beat line is not a tell on its own; it belongs with the Ch18 audit where its context can be judged.

findings.quote: Visual, Auditory, Kinesthetic — a three-channel model of how people represent experience internally and communicate externally. Taught in NLP, intelligence training, and performance contexts as a practical tool for building rapport and compliance through matched communication style.
findings.where: Ch17, VAK Pacing Framework glossary entry
findings.why: Reveal dash, an internally/externally balanced pair, a subjectless Taught in fragment, and an NLP/intelligence/performance tricolon of unnamed authorities, all in two sentences. The first reader counted the dash in the notes but never flagged the entry.
findings.rewrite: VAK stands for visual, auditory, kinesthetic: three channels people use to take in experience and talk about it. NLP trainers teach it, and so do some interrogation instructors, as a way to build rapport by matching how someone communicates.

findings.quote: look for nonverbal confirmation: a slight forward lean, a sharp blink, a microexpression of recognition. Only ask for a verbal yes when you already know the answer is yes. The audience hears the confirmation but not the process that led you there.
findings.where: Ch17, The Four Principles of Translation, 03 Watch before you speak
findings.why: Tricolon of signals then an aphoristic closer. On its own it passes, but it is the third of four numbered principles that each end on a one-line closer (1813 Use it that way. 1816 Everything that follows lands harder... 1822 ...entered something with real consequences.). Four for four is the template, not the man.
findings.rewrite: Before you ask for a yes out loud, look for the yes on their body: a lean in, a hard blink, that flicker of recognition. Then ask. The room only hears the confirmation.

findings.quote: readings land harder when the spectator is willing and silently holding a real question in mind, because meaning has a frame to organize itself around.
findings.where: Ch17, Context Is Never Neutral, ANTHEM_ARIA paraphrase
findings.why: meaning has a frame to organize itself around is an abstract noun doing the work. Attributed to Anthem and Aria but the phrasing is the paraphraser's. Also the literal placeholder tag ANTHEM_ARIA: is still sitting in the manuscript text here and at 1829.
findings.rewrite: Anthem and Aria add that a read lands harder when the spectator actually wants one and is holding a real question in their head, because now everything you say has something to attach to.

findings.quote: Read their writing not for content but for co-occurrence. Which words do they consistently place near each other? Which concepts are fused?
findings.where: Ch17, Collocation as a Pre-Show Tool
findings.why: not for X but for Y contrast followed by two matched rhetorical questions. The becomes a great covert method line just before it is authentic Chris, which makes the switch into model rhythm more noticeable.
findings.rewrite: Do not read their emails for what they say. Read them for which words keep landing next to each other.

findings.quote: Stock lines exist for a reason. They give a beginner structure, provide entry points into common personality categories, and help someone understand recurring emotional patterns before they have developed their observational range.
findings.where: Ch17, Stock Lines vs. Seeing the Person
findings.why: Two short punches to open, then a three-verb tricolon of long balanced clauses, then a But they become a liability turn. Even, mid-length, evenly weighted; the shape of a model paragraph rather than a working performer explaining why beginners use stock lines.
findings.rewrite: Stock lines are training wheels. They give a beginner something to say and a rough map of the common personality types until their eyes catch up. The problem starts when you keep leaning on them instead of looking at the person in front of you.

findings.quote: At one end is pure cold reading: no prior knowledge, no warm-up, working entirely from observation, context, and the Forer effect.
findings.where: Ch17, One Name, Three Different Skills
findings.why: no/no anaphora plus an entirely tricolon, and the whole sentence is then repeated nearly word for word in the spectrum diagram at 1799. Part of the same three-pass duplication the first reader caught at 1795 but did not anchor here.

chapter_notes: Ch17 (lines 1768-1920, about 3,540 words, 66 prose paragraphs). Contrast hammer is the dominant tic: roughly 36 'is not X. It is Y' / 'not X, Y' / 'not just' constructions, about one per 100 words. It peaks in the IF YOU REMEMBER NOTHING ELSE block (1903-1907) where five consecutive paragraphs each open on a negation and close on an aphorism.

Punch endings: 29 of 66 paragraphs close on a one-line aphoristic sentence (That is thin slicing. That difference is everything. That is the point. You let it land. One is noise.). Chris uses one per section; this chapter averages one per two paragraphs.
Tricolons: about 29, including the three identically shaped Visual/Auditory/Kinesthetic sentences at 1837 and the closing 'observing, reflecting, and delivering' at 1903.

Em dashes: 8 in the range, 5 of them the 'X — Y' reveal dash (1772, 1777, 1834, 1835) plus a paired aside at 1779 and one each in the chapter heading (1768) and VAK definition (1791). All should go under the standing rule.

Duplicate drafting is the structural tell: Thin Slicing is defined twice (1778-1780 and 1833-1835), the Forer Effect twice (1781-1782 and 1808-1809), the cold/warm/hot spectrum in prose (1794-1795) and again as a diagram (1797-1807), 'live observation rather than pure inference' appears verbatim three times, and 'one is noise / three is a read' appears at 1786 and 1894. The two Thin Slicing passages also disagree on clip length (six seconds at 1779 vs thirty then six at 1835). Reads like several AI passes merged without dedup.

Vague attribution cluster: ER nurses / trial lawyers / hostage negotiators (1780) unsourced; 'Widely used by performers and intelligence professionals' (1789); 'peer-reviewed literature, has clinical and forensic applications' (1835); 'high-stakes practitioner settings' (1838); 'Baker and his associates' (1886) for what is a nameable 2008 study. The Chase Hughes line at 1792 is framed as a quote ('put it plainly') but reads as paraphrase; verify before attributing.

Abstract nouns as agents: 'Plausibility does the rest' (1809), 'Delivery does. Specificity does.' (1903), 'The association becomes belief' (1886), 'meaning has a frame to organize itself around' (1826, contributor paraphrase). 'Architecture of' appears three times (1867, 1887, 1889); the book title may excuse one, not three in two pages.
The summary paragraph at 1906 introduces 'psychological force', which the chapter never discusses. Likely pasted from another chapter's summary; either cut it or move it.

The three Cold Reading in Practice vignettes (1875-1877) are constructed: no names, no venues, no dates, tense shifts between 'you approach' and 'he set down his drink', and staccato beats (Not surprise. Recognition. / Slight eyebrow flash. Head tilts. Wrong frame.). Chris's real anecdotes carry specifics; swapping in three actual shows would fix the cadence and the credibility at once.

The 'Chris Michael's Take' box (1832) is the most important single fix: it is labeled as his own voice and is built entirely from matched If/If sentences and a 'That is the difference between X and Y' closer.

What reads authentically Chris: the Anthem and Aria note at 1774 (2025 and 2026 APCA, close to three hundred shows in twenty countries, 'dear friend'), 'so much that you get sick of hearing it' at 1885, 'becomes a great covert method' at 1897, the self-correction 'Or at least, presents most consistently through one' at 1837, the numbered direct-instruction headings of the Four Principles, and the quoted reading scripts at 1890-1892 (those are performance lines and should stay as written). The ANTHEM_ARIA paraphrases (1826, 1829) are contributor content but the cadence is the paraphraser's, flagged with contributor=true.
Lists, the VAK table (1839-1865), the spectrum diagram (1796-1807), the KEY PRINCIPLE callout (1870), and the decision-tree bullets (1879-1883) were treated as structural and not flagged.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model, with Chris surfacing in maybe six places: the Anthem and Aria note with its APCA years and show counts, the counterintelligence sick of hearing it aside, becomes a great covert method, the Or at least self-correction in the VAK paragraph, and the quoted read scripts. Everything else is the model's chapter-writing rhythm, and the single most damaging habit is the contrast hammer used as the default sentence shape: roughly a dozen clean is not X / It is Y pairs plus another two dozen not-X-comma-Y and not-because/because variants, one every hundred words, peaking in the IF YOU REMEMBER NOTHING ELSE block where five straight paragraphs open on a negation and close on an aphorism. That habit does the most damage because it hollows out the teaching: every time the text says what cold reading is not, it spends a sentence it could have spent on a real room, a real person, a real line that landed or missed. The three Cold Reading in Practice vignettes are the clearest fix, since nameless, venue-less scenes told in staccato fragments are the opposite of how Chris tells a story; three actual shows would repair the cadence and the credibility at once. Second priority is the Chris Michael's Take box, which is labeled as his voice and currently sounds least like it. Also flag for production: two ANTHEM_ARIA: placeholder tags still in the text, eight em dashes, and a summary paragraph about psychological forces that belongs to some other chapter.

group.label: Ch18 Contact Mind Reading, Ch19 Hypnosis

findings.quote: You start moving. Not because you decided to. Not because anyone pushed you or pulled you.
findings.why: Two stacked "Not because" fragments right after "Not a big one" and "Loose. Easy. Not the grip" in the previous paragraph; the opener runs on negation fragments the way a model writes a lyrical second-person scene.
findings.where: Ch18 Contact Mind Reading, What It Feels Like
findings.rewrite: You start moving, and you did not decide to. Nobody pushed or pulled you. The direction just starts feeling more obvious than the alternatives.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Two stacked Not-because fragments plus genuinely and the slows/slow/stop staccato. On its own a medium tic; the high-severity problem is the whole 1925-1928 opener as a cluster, and the 1925 sentence the finder only mentioned in passing is added under missed.

findings.quote: never announced, never described, never pointed at. They saw hesitation that looked like searching and correction that looked like tuning and arrival that looked nothing like guessing. They do not have a word for what they saw. Which means you did your job.
findings.why: Triple anaphora, then a three-part polysyndeton, then a one-line punch closer. Three devices stacked in four sentences.
findings.rewrite: The audience watched someone walk through a room toward a target nobody ever named or pointed at. They saw a little hesitation, a couple of corrections, then an arrival that did not look like a guess. They have no word for it, and that is the job.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Triple anaphora, three-part polysyndeton, then a one-line punch. Unmistakable model closer for the What It Feels Like section.

findings.quote: Internal events do not stay internal for long. Under the right conditions, they become structure. A thought becomes a movement. A hidden target becomes a change in pressure through the wrist. A private intention begins leaking into physical behavior before language catches up.
findings.why: Abstract nouns as agents in a three-beat "X becomes Y" ladder, capped by a quotable line; and the first two sentences are repeated verbatim at line 1981, so the aphorism is used twice in one chapter (plus the epigraph says it a third way).
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. The paragraph starts in real Chris (loose grammar, I am sure you are surprised) and switches voice mid-paragraph. Under the right conditions appears twice inside this one paragraph and the aphorism returns verbatim at 1981.

findings.quote: Seen that way, contact mind reading is not separate from the rest of mentalism. It is one of the purest examples of the same rule. If the experience is designed properly, the body begins revealing what the mind is trying to hold.
findings.why: "Is not X. It is Y." followed by a mirrored aphorism (body reveals what mind holds). The whole paragraph is a summary flourish with no new information.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Whole paragraph is a hammer plus a mirrored aphorism and adds nothing the previous paragraph did not say.

findings.quote: The arm firms slightly. The hand resists. The body no longer wants to continue in that path. The method lives in that difference.
findings.why: Staccato triple then "The method lives in that difference," an abstract-noun-as-agent punch. Earlier in the same paragraph: "You are not listening for words, and you are not waiting for conscious assistance. You are feeling..." plus a six-item list.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. The kitchen-keys picture earlier in the paragraph is on-voice; the staccato triple and The method lives in that difference closer are the model. Medium because the paragraph carries real instruction.

findings.quote: The signal has not necessarily disappeared. Your ability to stay with it has.
findings.why: Elliptical mirrored punch closing a paragraph that already contains "the signal is not created by the participant alone. It is created inside a relationship" and "is not separate from movement planning." Three contrast hammers in one paragraph.
findings.where: Ch18, The Method (Trevo Sheikh point, paraphrased by Chris)
findings.rewrite: The signal is usually still there. What went missing is your attention.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Four contrast frames in one paragraph (not separate from, not created by the participant alone, not always a problem with the spectator, then this elliptical closer). Trevo's point is real; the wrapping is not.

findings.quote: That is a crucial shift in how to think about this. Contact mind reading is not only about what the participant sends. It is also about what the performer can remain quiet enough to detect. A strong performance state on your side is part of the method.
findings.why: "crucial" (AI vocabulary) plus a "not only X. It is also Y." pair plus a punch closer, all in a four-sentence paragraph that restates the previous one.
findings.rewrite: So the transmitter is only half of it. The other half is whether you can get quiet enough to feel what they are sending. Your own state is part of the method.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. crucial plus not-only/also plus punch closer, and the paragraph restates 1938. Nothing here is Chris.

findings.quote: That distinction matters. We are not only reading movement. We are reading organized intention.
findings.why: Signpost opener ("That distinction matters") into a "not only X. We are Y" hammer; "matters" as a sentence verb appears roughly ten times in this chapter.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. matters three times in four sentences, plus genuine and quietly, plus the not-only hammer. matters appears 22 times in this range.

findings.quote: The strongest transmitter is usually not the person straining the hardest. It is usually the person who can quietly hold the target, stay emotionally committed to it, and let the body do what it naturally does.
findings.why: Stand-alone one-paragraph aphorism: "not X. It is Y" plus a tricolon plus "quietly" (used four times in the range). Follows a paragraph ending on "clear intention organizes the body better than clutter does," another quotable.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Standalone aphorism paragraph immediately after 1946 which already closed on a quotable. Two closers back to back.

findings.quote: It is not. It is interactive. It depends not only on what the participant's body is doing, but on what the participant accepts, expects, and allows.
findings.why: Two-word negation fragment, then "It is interactive," then "not only... but," then a tricolon. The paragraph before (1949) already did "is not only dependent on... It is also highly dependent on."
findings.rewrite: It is not purely mechanical. It is a two-way thing. The body is doing its part, but so is what the spectator expects and what they are willing to go along with.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. It is not. It is interactive. then not-only/but then tricolon, one paragraph after 1949 did the same not-only/also move.

findings.quote: That line is not neutral. It is a suggestion. It gives the participant a role. It tells them what kind of experience they are about to have. It narrows interpretation. It creates expectancy.
findings.why: Six consecutive "It [verb]s" sentences after the one-line paragraph "He is right." This is the model's list-as-prose rhythm.
findings.where: Ch18, Suggestibility and the Frame (Peter Turner point, paraphrased)
findings.rewrite: He is right. That line is a suggestion. It hands the spectator a role and tells them what kind of experience they are about to have, and once they accept that split between conscious and unconscious, they tend to respond the way the effect needs.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Six consecutive It-verb sentences. List rendered as prose; nobody talks like this.

findings.quote: The spectator does better when they know, at least in broad terms, what is about to happen, what their job is, and what kind of internal experience to allow. In that sense, contact mind reading has a great deal in common with other suggestibility-based work. The participant is not only transmitting. They are entering a role.
findings.why: Tricolon, "In that sense," and a "not only X. They are Y" closer; this paragraph also opens with a second tricolon ("the path is clear, the frame is believable, and the participant understands").
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim (56 words, trim to the last two sentences). Two tricolons, In that sense, and a not-only closer. Pattern-y rather than egregious; the paragraph is doing legitimate connective work.

findings.quote: That does not mean every I-type is automatically ideal, and it does not mean other types cannot work well. It means that when suggestibility, responsiveness, and willingness matter, that style of participant often gives you better odds.
findings.why: "That does not mean X. It means Y" formula, repeated at 1964, 2017, and 2025. Plus a tricolon.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. The does-not-mean/It-means formula recurs at 1964, 2017, 2025, 2081 (6 hits in range). The I-type advice itself is real content.

findings.quote: Someone who easily follows a simple imagination exercise. Someone who reacts well in a pendulum or suggestibility test. Someone who does not seem embarrassed to play along. Someone who accepts your framing quickly rather than interrogating it.
findings.why: Five "Someone who" fragments in a row presented as prose. Would be fine as a bulleted list; as paragraph prose it reads generated.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Five Someone-who fragments as prose. A bulleted list would be fine; as a paragraph it reads generated.

findings.quote: a participant who is suggestible enough to accept the frame, responsive enough to inhabit the role, and motivated enough to let the process happen.
findings.why: "So yes, X can be discussed through [tricolon]. All of that is real and important. But..." then this three-part parallel, then a one-line paragraph aphorism at 1959 ("The body may reveal the path, but suggestion often clears it."). Full model closer sequence.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. So yes X, all of that is real, but Y concession pivot into a three-part parallel and then the 1959 one-line aphorism paragraph. Full model closing sequence.

findings.quote: This is where performance technique matters more than many books admit. Contact mind reading is not only something you do. It is something you set up.
findings.why: "matters more than many books admit" inflation, then the "not only X. It is Y" hammer as a full paragraph. Two paragraphs later: "Emotional investment also matters more than many performers realize." Same move twice in a row.
findings.rewrite: You set this up before you ever touch a wrist. Most books skip that part.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. matters more than many books admit inflation into a not-only hammer as an entire paragraph, then the same inflation two paragraphs later.

findings.quote: They care whether you succeed. Their attention sharpens. Their internal orientation toward the object becomes stronger. In practice, that can make the signal cleaner.
findings.why: Three short parallel sentences and a hedged punch. Opens with "matters more than many performers realize."
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. The hide-something-that-matters advice is good and practical; the three-beat staccato closer is the tic.

findings.quote: Many performances improve not because the participant changes, but because the performer gets better at shaping the conditions.
findings.why: "not because X, but because Y" closer on a paragraph that already has a tricolon ("clearer structure, stronger expectation, or better guidance"). Trevo's observation is real content; the wrapping is model.
findings.where: Ch18, Setting Up the Conditions (Trevo Sheikh point, paraphrased)
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. One not-because/but-because closer; would be low alone but it is the sixth contrast hammer in this section.

findings.quote: You want a hold that is stable, sensitive, and quiet. Too loose and the information becomes vague. Too forceful and you create resistance that drowns out what you are trying to feel.
findings.why: Tricolon plus mirrored "Too X... Too Y..." pair, then "not only controls... but also allows you to feel any subtle signals, tugs, or pushes" (another not-only plus tricolon) to close.
findings.where: Ch18, The Grip (Trevo's grip, described by Chris)
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Too loose/Too forceful is ordinary coaching language and the paragraph has real specifics (Trevo's arm-under-arm grip). Only the stable/sensitive/quiet tricolon and the not-only/but-also closer are tics.

findings.quote: Move away. Re-approach. Change angle. Compare the signal against nearby alternatives. Often the right target becomes clearer through contrast. Verification is not a sign of insecurity. It is part of good method.
findings.why: Imperative fragment triple then a "not X. It is Y" closer. The section heading "Verify, Verify, Verify" and the one-line paragraph "Then verify it again" above it make this the third triple in a row.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Imperative fragments are within Chris's range (compare the coaching lines at 1965); the Verification is not a sign of insecurity. It is part of good method. hammer and the more deceptive, not less tailing negation at 1973 are the model.

findings.quote: Thought becomes tension. Intention becomes direction. Uncertainty becomes drag. Confidence becomes continuation.
findings.why: Four abstract-noun equations in a row ending a paragraph. Nobody talks like this; it is the model's signature rhythm. Preceded by "the mechanism is quieter and more physical."
findings.where: Ch18, The Science Behind Contact Mind Reading
findings.rewrite: What you are feeling is the body getting ready around a target the spectator is holding in their head. Doubt shows up as drag. Certainty shows up as the arm getting easier to move.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Four abstract-noun equations in a row. The single most recognizable model rhythm in Ch18.

findings.quote: Suggestibility matters. Expectation matters. Emotional investment matters. The performer's attentional stability matters. The participant's willingness to let the process happen matters. The method is physical, yes, but the conditions that make it work are psychological and relational.
findings.why: Five "X matters" sentences in a row plus a "physical, yes, but psychological and relational" antithesis closer. The opening line ("I would still be careful not to reduce the whole thing to a laboratory sentence") is Chris; the rest of the paragraph is not.
findings.where: Ch18, The Science Behind Contact Mind Reading
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Five bare X matters sentences plus a physical-yes-but-psychological antithesis. The opening laboratory sentence line is Chris; the rest is not.

findings.quote: If you frame it too mystically, you risk claiming more than the method can honestly support. If you frame it too mechanically, you flatten the wonder. The strongest framing usually sits in the middle. Focused thought genuinely changes the body, and touch lets another person feel those changes in real time. That is already fascinating enough.
findings.why: Mirrored conditionals, "sits in the middle," "genuinely," and a five-word punch closer. Textbook balanced-antithesis paragraph.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim (56 words, trim). Mirrored conditionals, sits in the middle, genuinely, five-word punch. Textbook balanced antithesis.

findings.quote: Anxiety, over-analysis, and constant self-monitoring make you less sensitive, not more. The performer who is obsessed with success and failure often misses the signal that was present all along. The performer who stays calm, curious, and playful usually feels more.
findings.why: Two tricolons, a tailing "not more," and a mirrored "The performer who... / The performer who..." pair, in three sentences.
findings.rewrite: Getting out of your own head is part of the technique. If you are grading yourself the whole time you go numb to the signal. The calm, curious version of you feels more. That is it.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Two tricolons, a tailing not more, and a mirrored The-performer-who pair in three sentences. The getting out of your own head opener is fine.

findings.quote: In that sense, contact mind reading teaches the same lesson as much of mentalism. Internal events do not stay internal for long. Under the right conditions, they become structure. And under the right conditions, another human being can feel that structure as it forms.
findings.why: Verbatim repeat of the 1931 aphorism, now with "under the right conditions" anaphora and an abstract closer. The chapter says this same sentence three times (epigraph, 1931, here).
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Third statement of the same aphorism in one chapter, now with under-the-right-conditions anaphora.

findings.quote: Research on movement and motor preparation supports the broader principle: intention changes the body early. Action planning alters readiness before overt movement appears, and prior intent can shape the kinematics of reaching and grasping before contact is ever made.
findings.why: "Research on movement and motor preparation supports" with no name or study, followed by "the useful rule is not that one cue proves intent, but that behavior has to be read in context." The paragraph opens in authentic Chris ("It makes me laugh to even think about that happening") and then switches voice mid-paragraph.
findings.where: Ch18, Intent Cues Beyond the Stage
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Research on movement and motor preparation supports with no name, kinematics jargon, then a not-that/but-that closer, all inside a paragraph that opened in authentic Chris (It makes me laugh).

findings.quote: I do not know who originated that term, but there is a real literature behind the principle. Anticipatory coarticulation (the way the mouth begins preparing for an upcoming sound before that sound is physically produced) is well documented.
findings.why: "there is a real literature" and "is well documented" with nothing cited, inside an otherwise authentic paragraph ("My dear friend Peter Turner"). Also "Lipping can fall into that category" and "that can function as an intent cue" read as hedged model summary.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. I do not know who originated that term is a genuinely human admission; only there is a real literature and is well documented are unsourced tells. Low, keep for the vague-attribution tally.

findings.quote: Once you can see the difference between an easy answer and a hunted one, you are no longer just watching thought. You are shaping what the search reveals.
findings.why: "no longer just X. You are Y" closer. Also does not belong to this chapter: nothing in Ch18 is about easy versus hunted answers or searches; it reads like a chapter closer generated for a memory-search chapter and pasted here.
findings.where: Ch18, chapter closer after the section break
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. no longer just X. You are Y closer, and the content (easy answer vs hunted one, what the search reveals) matches nothing in Ch18. This is an orphaned closer pasted under the wrong section break; mechanical fix, not just voice.

findings.quote: "Hypnosis is not what you think it is. That is why it works."
findings.why: Epigraph built on the "not X. That is why Y" formula; structural, but it sets up a chapter whose every section ends the same way.
findings.where: Ch19 How Hypnosis Really Works, epigraph
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Epigraph is structural, but the wording is the exact formula the chapter closes on at 2096, so the bookends confess the pattern. Keep as low so Chris sees the pair.

findings.quote: The lights were responded to. The lane changes happened. The car is parked correctly. You drove competently for twenty minutes and experienced none of it consciously — your attention was somewhere else entirely, absorbed in its own interior weather.
findings.why: Passive fragment stack ("were responded to"), an em dash reveal, "interior weather," "entirely," then "It requires no script, no watch, no performance" tricolon. The only prose em dash in the range.

Everything else is 'one of the most replicated ideas', 'researchers have found', 'one of the most important findings in hypnosis neuroscience', 'medical organizations began recognizing its value', 'you can see this in imaging studies', 'EEG studies often point to', 'Some work has linked'. Repeats ~7x.

Ch19 the 'X is more interesting than Y' inflation move appears four times across the range (1931 'more interesting than people think', 2019 'The truth is more interesting than either extreme', 2022 'far more interesting than the stage version', 2090 'the more fascinating it gets').

Ch19 the last three blocks (Closing Thought 2090-2092, Chris Michael's Take 2094, closer 2096) are three consecutive aphorism stacks with zero first person and zero specifics; the Take in particular reads as the model's voice under Chris's name. Same for the alcohol section, which is three one-line paragraphs in a row followed by a six-sentence antithesis ladder.

Ch19 tricolons: about 25 strict triples plus a heavy four-item habit ('attention, prediction, perception, and self-monitoring'; 'language, biology, expectation, and experience'; 'allocates attention, weighs incoming information, monitors the self, and predicts experience'). 'genuine/genuinely' appears four times in two sentences at 2026.

Ch19 what reads authentically Chris: the dreams hook at 2008 ('I have always found it strange that people doubt hypnosis while unquestioningly accepting something far more bizarre: dreams'); the Cold War memo framing at 2014 ('I first encountered the following quote through my intelligence work, and I am at liberty to share it here') and the intelligence-world aside at 2017 about hypnosis coming up matter-of-factly next to elicitation and rapport building; the car-window / streetlight memory at 2047 and 'most performers roll their eyes at it' at 2052; the numbers at 2042 (ten to fifteen percent, stable over decades). There is no performance story, venue, or named show anywhere in the hypnosis chapter, which is unusual for Chris and is the biggest missing voice signal.

Em dashes in range: 3 total, two in chapter headers (1921, 2001) and one in prose at 2005. Curly quotes and curly apostrophes are mixed with straight ones throughout (participant's vs brain’s), which is consistent with pasted AI output next to hand edits.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model that was handed Chris's material. The ideas are his (the dreams hook, the Cold War memo, the car-window memory, the I-type selection advice, the Trevo, Satori, and Peter Turner points, the ten-to-fifteen-percent figure) and the handful of unmistakably human lines survive (Cool, huh?, It makes me laugh to even think about that happening, My dear friend Peter Turner, You may be surprised to see a T1 label here, the coaching lines at 1965), but almost every paragraph is closed by the same machine. The single most damaging habit is the contrast hammer used as a paragraph ender: It is not X. It is Y. and its cousins (not only/merely/just 12 times, does not mean / It means 6 times, plus a couple dozen bare is-not/It-is pairs), so that roughly one paragraph in two across both chapters lands on an identical two-beat, with matters as a bare verb 22 times and genuine/genuinely 9 times riding along. Ch19 is the worse offender because it bookends itself with the formula four times (epigraph, Closing Thought, Chris Michael's Take, closer) and the Take has no first person, no show, and no specific at all under his own name. Two mechanical fixes should come before any voice rewrite: delete one of the duplicate What It Feels Like drafts at 2005/2006, and move or cut the orphaned Ch18 closer at 1989, which refers to a hunted answer and a search that appear nowhere in the chapter. All 61 of the first reader's quotes are verbatim and none is a heading, list, or contributor's own words, so I kept all 61 with a few re-grades downward (1969, 1986, 2063, 2068 to low; 1926, 1954, 2012, 2038-adjacent items to medium) and added six the finder cited only in passing or missed outright, the worst being the alcohol section's three consecutive one-line paragraphs at 2084-2087.

group.label: Ch20 Babel Count, Ch21 Psychological Forces (first part)

findings.quote: the force is not really about safewords at all. It is about retrieval. It is about knowing that the first thing a person says is not always the first thing they ever knew.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK
findings.why: Three negative parallelisms and an "It is about... It is about..." anaphora stacked as the paragraph's closer, followed by one more quotable line. This is the model's summary move, not Chris landing a point.
findings.rewrite: So the safeword part is just the hook. What you are really using is retrieval. The first word out of someone's mouth is whichever one was easiest to reach right then, not the one they know best.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Closes the worst paragraph in the range with a triple negative parallelism plus 'It is about... It is about...' anaphora, then one more quotable line. Pure model summary move.

findings.quote: Repetition increases familiarity. Familiarity increases fluency. And fluency changes what feels easy, natural, and immediate to retrieve.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK
findings.why: Anadiplosis staircase (repetition to familiarity to fluency) capped with a tricolon. Textbook model opener for an explanation paragraph.
findings.rewrite: The more you hear something, the faster it comes back to you. That is the whole engine here.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Anadiplosis staircase (repetition > familiarity > fluency) capped by a tricolon, opening a section titled THE PSYCHOLOGY BEHIND IT. Nothing in Chris's corpus builds sentences this way.

findings.quote: you are not inserting a thought like a computer command. You are setting conditions that make some thoughts easier to reach than others.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK
findings.why: Fourth "not X. You are Y" contrast in a single paragraph, immediately followed by the aphorism "spontaneity is often just the name we give to a process whose bias we did not feel happening." Density is the tell.
findings.rewrite: You are not planting the word. You are just making it the easiest one to grab.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. On its own a medium, but it is the third 'not X. You are Y' in one paragraph and leads straight into the spontaneity aphorism. Density is the tell, as the brief says.

findings.quote: That is too crude. What seems closer to the truth is this: your phrasing provides a partial cue, and the brain completes the rest from cultural knowledge.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK
findings.why: "What seems closer to the truth is this:" is the persuasive-authority trope from the taxonomy (cutting through to a deeper truth, then restating an ordinary claim). Sits between two more aphoristic beats.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. 'What seems closer to the truth is this:' is the persuasive-authority trope from the taxonomy, and the two-word fragment 'That is too crude.' sets it up. The 'neat little drawer labeled banana safeword' joke before it is the only Chris-like beat and should survive the rewrite.

findings.quote: people rely on what memory researchers call scripts — organized patterns that help us fill in gaps
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK
findings.why: "Memory researchers" with no name, plus an em dash definition. Same paragraph also has "The hippocampus is heavily implicated in pattern completion" with no source. The book uses evidence tiers; this reads like model gap-filling.
findings.rewrite: Schank and Abelson called these scripts back in the 70s: the stock pattern your brain uses to fill in what a situation is supposed to look like.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. 'Memory researchers call' is nameless attribution with an em dash definition. The book uses evidence tiers, so this reads as gap-fill. Schank and Abelson is the correct named source if Chris keeps the sentence.

findings.quote: That is why this force matters. It reveals something deeper than a cute coincidence. It recruits whatever culture, memory, fluency, and association have already made available, then times the question so the answer arrives before competing answers fully assemble.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK
findings.why: "That is why this force matters" plus "something deeper than" is significance inflation; the four-item abstract list (culture, memory, fluency, association) is the model's comprehensive-sounding roll call.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Upgrading from medium: 'That is why this force matters' + 'something deeper than' is significance inflation, followed by a four-noun roll call and the lyrical 'before competing answers fully assemble'. Three tells in three sentences right after the one authentic line ('We just can't. It is truly impossible.').

findings.quote: In live exchange, you are not only giving content. You are giving cadence, tone, expectation, immediacy, and social framing. The spectator is not calmly browsing memory. They are responding. And in that response window, the easiest answer often wins.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, A NOTE ON PERFORMING THIS
findings.why: "Not only X. You are giving Y" with a five-noun list, then a second negative parallelism, a two-word fragment, and a punch closer. Every device in the brief in one paragraph.
findings.rewrite: Said out loud, this hits harder than almost any psychological force I know. In person they do not get to sit and browse. They have to answer you right now, and the easiest word wins.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. 'Not only X. You are giving Y' with a five-noun list, second negative parallelism, two-word fragment, punch closer. Every device in the brief in five sentences. The opening 'Spoken aloud, this can hit harder than almost any psychological force I have come across' is Chris and worth keeping.

findings.quote: Reading is flatter. The words arrive, but not always with urgency. Not always with rhythm. Not always with the tiny pressures that come from hearing a human voice choose one phrase over another
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, A NOTE ON PERFORMING THIS
findings.why: "Not always... Not always... Not always" fragment stack building to a long lyrical clause. Staccato drama from the taxonomy.
findings.rewrite: On the page it is flatter. There is no voice speeding up on one word and slowing down on the next, so the reader never feels the push.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. 'Not always... Not always... Not always' fragment stack swelling into a long lyrical clause. Staccato drama, taxonomy section 31.

findings.quote: On the page, the reader has distance. In conversation, the spectator has momentum. And momentum is where this force lives.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, A NOTE ON PERFORMING THIS
findings.why: Mirrored two-clause contrast then anadiplosis (momentum / momentum) into a quotable aphorism. Third consecutive paragraph built on the same contrast-plus-punch skeleton.
findings.rewrite: In conversation they answer fast because you are standing right there. On the page nothing is pushing them.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Mirrored contrast then anadiplosis into 'momentum is where this force lives'. The phone observation that follows in the same paragraph (with the contraction 'doesn't') is real field experience and is the seed for the rewrite.

findings.quote: Culture does not spread only through direct viewing. It spreads through repetition, paraphrase, secondhand reference, clips, jokes, headlines, and the thousands of tiny echoes that detach an idea from its original home and turn it into ambient cultural residue.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, My Current Favorite Psychological Force
findings.why: Negative parallelism opening a seven-item list that ends on a coined abstraction ("ambient cultural residue"). Then the paragraph closes on "By the time you ask the question, the work may already be half done." Model rhythm start to finish.
findings.rewrite: They do not need to have seen either clip. Jokes get repeated, quoted, and clipped until nobody remembers where they came from. By the time you ask, the word is already sitting there.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Negative parallelism launching a seven-item list that lands on the coined abstraction 'ambient cultural residue', then two aphoristic closers. The Family Guy and Kevin Hart specifics in the previous paragraph are Chris; this paragraph is the model explaining them.

findings.quote: The word does not just mean something—it feels like something.
findings.where: Ch21 Psychological Forces, catalog entry 07 Phonetic
findings.why: "Does not just X, it Y" with an unspaced em dash reveal. The single most recognizable model construction, inside an otherwise structural catalog line.
findings.rewrite: Words have a sound and a texture as well as a meaning, and similar sounds pull similar words up.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Inside a structural catalog line, but the wording itself is the single most recognizable model construction (does not just X, unspaced em dash, it Y). Catalog exemption does not cover it.

findings.quote: People mirror structure more than instruction. You are not telling them how to think. You are showing them how thinking looks.
findings.where: Ch20 The Babel Count, Setting the Rhythm
findings.why: Aphorism opener, then a "not X. You are Y" mirror with a poetic flourish ("how thinking looks"). Reads as a quotable card, not Chris explaining a method.
findings.rewrite: They copy what you do more than what you say. You spelled a word out loud with a nod on each letter, so that is how they will spell theirs. It works as long as you have not put them on guard.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Aphorism opener plus 'not telling them how to think / showing them how thinking looks' mirror. The two plain sentences that follow ('When they take their turn, they follow it...') are Chris and show the contrast.

findings.quote: People believe they are thinking freely. They are not.
findings.where: Ch20 The Babel Count, The Key Insight
findings.why: Standalone one-line paragraph with tailing negation, immediately followed at 2127 by the staircase "That structure has a pace. Pace is measurable." Two model devices back to back under a heading called The Key Insight.
findings.rewrite: They think they are spelling freely. They are actually spelling at the pace you just showed them, and you can count that pace.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. One-line paragraph directly under a heading called The Key Insight, tailing negation, immediately followed by the 2127 staircase. Fragmented-header pattern plus staccato drama.

findings.quote: They are following a structure you gave them. That structure has a pace. Pace is measurable.
findings.where: Ch20 The Babel Count, The Key Insight
findings.why: Anadiplosis chain (structure to pace to measurable) in three shrinking sentences. The final clause "the method becomes very easy and approachable" is the authentic Chris bit; the setup is not.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Structure > pace > measurable anadiplosis in three shrinking sentences. 'Once you understand that, the method becomes very easy and approachable' at the end is the authentic clunky Chris line.

findings.quote: A finger taps. A head nods. A rhythm forms. They are not doing this for you. They are doing it to keep track.
findings.where: Ch20 The Babel Count, The Basic Idea
findings.why: Three-fragment tricolon straight into a negative parallelism. Same paragraph repeats the trick at its end (see 2114 second finding), so the whole paragraph is bookended by model rhythm.
findings.rewrite: Watch them and you will see a finger tapping or a little nod on each letter. They are not doing it for you. It is how they keep their place.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Three-fragment tricolon straight into a negative parallelism, opening the paragraph. Bookended by a second tricolon (index 15). The paragraph's last sentence about the tool belt is Chris.

findings.quote: A nod marks a step. A finger marks a step. A breath marks a step. You are going to use that function.
findings.where: Ch20 The Babel Count, The Basic Idea
findings.why: Second tricolon in the same paragraph, this time as strict anaphora. "The thought becomes physical" two sentences earlier is the aphorism that sets it up.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Strict three-line anaphora, set up two sentences earlier by 'The thought becomes physical.' Two tricolons in one paragraph is unmistakable.

findings.quote: What you do not know — what no one expects you to know — is what day of the week that date falls on. That is the detail most people would never think to calculate, which makes it the detail that lands hardest.
findings.where: Ch20 The Babel Count, The Birthday Application
findings.why: Paired em dash suspension for drama, then a mirrored "the detail... the detail" aphorism. Chris punctuates with commas, colons, and parentheses, never this.
findings.rewrite: You already have the month, day and year. The one thing nobody expects you to know is what day of the week they were born on. Almost nobody has ever worked that out, which is exactly why it hits so hard.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Paired em dash suspension for drama, then the mirrored 'the detail... the detail' aphorism. Chris punctuates with commas, colons, ellipses, and parentheses, never a double dash interruption.

findings.quote: The method only costs you if you reveal its edges. Keep the frame small. Let the reveal break out of it.

findings.why: Callout box opens with "Never show your ceiling early" and closes on three consecutive aphorisms. Even in a box, four fortune-cookie lines in a row is the model.

findings.quote: You are not guessing the season. You are describing it through its associations. They hear their own mental images reflected back to them, and the method disappears entirely. It reads as deep perceptual access, not arithmetic.

findings.quote: Influence and counting. That is the whole secret of The Babel Count.

findings.rewrite: That is really all The Babel Count is. You set the rhythm, then you count.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Two-noun fragment plus 'That is the whole secret' is the exact 'That is the whole game' closer formula. Chapter ends on a model sign-off.

findings.quote: This is not about guessing. This is timing and body language together.

Just enough to establish a pattern' is a stage direction any teacher writes; it is the most natural of the chapter's contrasts and flagging it dilutes the real hits. findings.why: Three em dashes in one paragraph (also "exactly — but they got close" and "banana — it seems it did land"). The content is authentic Chris procedure; only the punctuation is the model's.

The content and the 'Speaking of solid ground' callback are Chris; the three em dashes in one paragraph (including 'exactly — but they got close' and 'banana — it seems it did land') are the model's punctuation and break the standing rule. Punctuation fix, not a voice rewrite.

findings.verifier_reason: Dropped. This is a stage-direction block inside a scripted routine ('Performer:' / 'Spectator:'), structural by the brief's rules, and the wording is concrete rather than machine-y. 'Shock, then applause' is ordinary blocking.

findings.why: Contrast question then a rule-of-three recipe. The neighboring Pros line (2254) adds "Feels organic and genuinely psychological" with the adverb tic.
