chapter_notes: Ch20 The Babel Count (2108-2167): the procedural core (2111-2140) is mostly Chris's teaching voice. Authentic tells: "Additionally, we want to increase the reliability of this so it can be a common tool in our tool belt" (clunky and human, leave it), "If this seems too advanced, instruct them to open their eyes", "plus or minus one letter if you are not yet well practiced", the STRAWBERRY demo script, and the real Fraser Parker / Obsidian credit. The model's fingerprint is structural: five single-sentence paragraphs used as pivots in 25 lines (2121, 2126, 2129, 2132, 2137) and a closer on almost every subsection ("That is it", "the rest is counting", "That margin is workable", "you have an opening", "not arithmetic", "That is the whole secret"). About 12 punch endings in 60 lines.

Ch20 negative parallelism repeats ~10x in this chapter (2111, 2114, 2119, 2122, 2124, 2126, 2159, 2161 twice, 2167). The five worst are quoted; the rest are the same shape. Fragment tricolons cluster in one paragraph (2114 has two).

Ch20 from Days of the Week onward (2150-2167) reads much more model-written than the first half: 7 of the chapter's 10 prose em dashes are in 2150-2162, plus "genuinely", "entirely" twice, the mirrored "the detail... the detail" line, and a KEY PRINCIPLE box made of four aphorisms. The birthday and season ideas are strong Chris material; the wording around them needs his hand.

Ch21 Psychological Forces, opening through Performance Note (2181-2197): reads authentically Chris and should be left mostly alone. Named sources (Emma Wooding, Peter Turner Propless Vol 7, Banachek), the phone-call story ("Peter threw this at me and I thought it was fantastic"), "that is right on target!", "off to the races", the fundraiser auction / spouse safeword framing, and the honest hedge that it works less well in text. This is the voice the rest of the range should be rewritten toward.

Ch21 line 2199 (WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK) is the single most machine-written paragraph in the range and the top rewrite priority: staircase opener, two nameless attributions ("memory researchers call", "hippocampus is heavily implicated"), "What seems closer to the truth is this:", four negative parallelisms, an "It is about... It is about" anaphora, and the aphorism "spontaneity is often just the name we give to a process whose bias we did not feel happening." One line inside it is unmistakably Chris and worth building the rewrite around: "Remember, humans cannot be random. We just can't. It is truly impossible." Either name a real source for scripts and pattern completion or cut those sentences.

Ch21 A NOTE ON PERFORMING THIS (2200-2205): three consecutive paragraphs share one skeleton (mirrored contrast, then a one-line aphoristic closer: "momentum is where this force lives", "the easiest answer often wins") plus a "Not always" x3 anaphora. The one authentic sentence is the phone tip ("It also doesn't seem to hold up well on the phone as people will tend to name whatever object they can see or last interacted with"), which is a real field observation with a contraction in it. Keep that, rebuild the rest around it.

Ch21 tossed-out deck and reputation maker (2206-2223): procedural and Chris-sounding ("Lean into your acting skills and pretend to get a cue from each", "You really don't have to overjustify it. Even that leans more toward over-explanation than I am usually comfortable with", "Annnnnd change it"). Only punctuation needs cleaning: 2211 alone has three em dashes, and 2207, 2209, 2214, 2222 have one each. Not flagged individually beyond 2211.

Ch21 catalog (2225-2300): structural and mostly exempt, but the template is model-shaped. Every "How to construct" line is exactly three rhetorical questions (9 of 9), most "Pros" lines are tricolons or fragment stacks ("Very high hit rate. Easy to understand. Good for demonstrating the principle." / "private, emotional, and real"), and the "How they work" lines end on mini-aphorisms (2245, 2253, 2261 "stay mentally warm", 2275). Adverb tics: "quietly biases", "quiet default", "genuinely psychological". Suggest keeping the grid but roughening the wording so the nine entries do not share one rhythm, and replacing 2278's "does not just mean something—it feels like something" outright.

Range-wide em dash breakdown for the count below: 29 total, of which 7 are the days-of-week table rows (2143-2149), 2 are chapter title lines (2108, 2179), and 20 are in prose or scripts. Plus one en dash (2273 "2–3"). All 21 prose and script dashes violate the standing no-dash rule regardless of voice.
group_verdict: This stretch is genuinely mixed, and the seam is easy to see. The procedural core of The Babel Count (the STRAWBERRY demo, 0.6 to 0.7 seconds per letter, plus or minus one letter, the weekday-not-weekend adjustment), the Peter Turner phone call, the fundraiser auction framing, the tossed-out-deck handling, and the Annnnnd change it script all read like Chris teaching. Everything wrapped around that material does not: the Key Insight box, the two KEY PRINCIPLE callouts, the chapter closer, the WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL FORCES WORK paragraph at 2199, and the three-paragraph A NOTE ON PERFORMING THIS are the model explaining Chris's ideas back to him. The single most damaging habit is the contrast-and-punch paragraph skeleton: a negative parallelism ('You are not X. You are Y.') that resolves into a one-line quotable closer. It appears roughly ten times in Ch20 and four times inside 2199 alone, and it is what turns a good field method into something that sounds like a keynote slide. The anadiplosis staircases (2127, 2199 opener, 2204) and the one-sentence pivot paragraphs under headings are the same habit in a different costume. Fix 2199 to 2205 first, then strip the closers off each Ch20 subsection, and the rest of the range is mostly a dash cleanup.

chapter_notes: Ch21 Psychological Forces (rest, lines 2301-2410): The force catalog (entries 10-13) is structural and mostly fine, but note that every How-to-construct entry is exactly three questions, which is a rule-of-three template. The essay sections between the catalog and the Jakob Michaels force (HOW FORCES COMBINE through Five Moving Parts, lines 2337-2383) are the worst stretch: 11 negative-parallelism constructions in about 45 lines, and roughly 12 paragraphs in a row that end on a one-line punch (The stack is not. / Stack them. / It is the framing. / permission, not elimination. / It just does not fit the job. / Build your fallback... / Build the fallback first. Every time. / That is the goal...). The same slogan gets reused as the closer of one paragraph and the opener of the next twice (sounds like a test / feels like a test at 2355 and 2357; build the fallback at 2364 and 2366). The not-broken template appears here (2360) and again in Ch21A (2439).

Ch21 Psychological Forces, Jakob Michaels section (lines 2397-2410): This is the most authentically Chris prose in the range and should be protected. Signals: friend named by full name, admits he was fooled, loose grammar (It felt that he truly read my mind), truly used four times, rhetorical question with a human tone (Who would want to imagine sadness or hatred deep in their heart?), We are dealing with psychology after all, back track as two words, pretty airtight. Two things inside it read pasted-in: the vmPFC parenthetical at 2406 and the one-sentence cognition map at 2408. Everything else there should stay as is.

Ch21A Predictive Text (lines 2411-2456): Alternates between two voices paragraph by paragraph. The practical how-to paragraphs (2423, 2425, 2426, 2430, 2433, 2438, 2441, 2442, 2443, 2447) are Chris: rambling instructions, maybe four or five of them, Marc Sueper's Mentyx name drop, I will be releasing a project, If you really want to be foolproof. The framing and summary paragraphs (2418-2421, 2436, 2439, 2454, 2456) are the model: not-random / it-is contrast, tricolons, gap-is-where-this-lives closers, and the poster-line chapter ending. The die/coin/truth facts appear twice (2437 and 2445) and One important note appears twice (2438 and 2446), which points to two drafts stitched together; one copy of each should be cut. The real Chris ending for this chapter is already written at 2433 (Until then, I thought it might be useful for you to get some ideas and have fun); the aphorism at 2456 could simply be deleted.

Em dashes: 7 total in the range, but 6 are in structural headings (Force Strength table levels and the 21A chapter title lines). Only one is in running prose (2326). Adverb tics in prose: completely 6x, genuinely 3x, entirely 2x, truly 5x (the truly hits are all in the Jakob section and read human), plus one Additionally, one essentially, one particularly, one precisely, one fundamental.
group_verdict: This stretch is two books stitched together. The catalog entries, the Jakob Michaels section, and the hands-on predictive text paragraphs (My favorite, fireworks, apple, Mentyx, the temporary chat tip, the Peter Turner credit) read like Chris: loose grammar, named friends, admitting he got fooled, instructions that ramble in a useful way. Everything that frames or summarizes those sections reads like the model, and the tell is not vocabulary but the way paragraphs end. From HOW FORCES COMBINE through Five Moving Parts (2337 to 2383) nearly every paragraph closes on a two-beat contrast slogan in the shape not X / It is Y (The stack is not. / It is the framing. / tone, not logic. / permission, not elimination. / It just does not fit the job. / It is five things working together. / They experience their own thought arriving.), often with the slogan repeated as the next paragraph's opener, and Ch21A reproduces the same habit at its open (not random / it is consistent) and close (a force waiting to be recognized). That contrast-hammer closer is the single most damaging habit here: it is the rhythm a reader who knows Chris's stage voice would hear as a slide deck, and because it lands on paragraph after paragraph rather than once per section, no amount of word swapping fixes it; those paragraphs need to be retold as Chris would say them to a friend, with the framework kept and the closers cut.

chapter_notes: Ch22 rhythm: the dominant tell is not vocabulary but the contrast hammer. I count roughly 33 negative-parallel constructions in 175 lines ("isn't X. It's Y", "not X but Y", "You're not X. You're Y"). The worst cluster is Premise Architecture (2491-2499), where five consecutive paragraphs each contain one and the KEY PRINCIPLE box repeats the section opener verbatim.

Ch22 section-opener template: eight sections in a row open with a one-line definitional hook or a reveal-shaped negative parallelism (2520 Covert Acquisition, 2526 Natural Language, 2538 Discarded Method, 2545 Time as Deception, 2552 The Pump, 2557 Direction/Depth/Distraction, 2568 Controlled Miss, 2573 Endgame Control). Any one is fine. Eight is a template. Vary them: start some sections in the middle of a story or with a direct instruction.

Ch22 paragraph endings: about 29 paragraphs in the range end on a one-line aphoristic punch. Silence Can Be Better Than Applause (2578-2583) is the peak, with every paragraph ending on a quotable and paragraph 2581 stacking four of them. Chris's real pattern (per the voice file) is long analytical paragraph, one short punch, long again. Here it is punch, punch, punch.

Repeated closer phrase: "knows the difference even when they can't name it" (2483) and "feel the difference even when they can't name what changed" (2554). Same model line generated twice. Also duplicated content pairs: 2481/2488 ("lives inside one of three failures"), 2491/2495 (premise/frame), 2520/2521 (rapport/humor/logistics). These are stitch seams from multiple generated drafts.

Ch22 anadiplosis and climax chains ("When the method feels natural, the performer feels natural. When the performer feels natural, the audience relaxes..." at 2533; "fragments, and fragments don't satisfy" 2477; "theories where contradictory theories collapse" 2475; "a procedure, and watching a procedure" 2487; "the performance becomes visible" 2609) appear about 6x. Chris does not chain clauses this way in any register in the voice file.

Ch22 intensifier tic: "genuinely" / "genuine" 8x across the range (2474, 2539, 2542, 2547, 2569, 2615, 2616), "entirely" 7x, "actually" 10x. "Genuinely brilliant", "genuinely changed", "genuinely inexplicable", "genuinely unclear" is the model reaching for sincerity. Chris's own hype is specific ("way fucking cooler than I thought"), not adverbial.

Ch22 structural seams worth fixing while rewriting: the heading says DIRECTION, DEPTH, AND DISTRACTION but the body runs direction, distraction, depth (2559-2562); the near-miss paragraph (2582) sits in the Silence section but belongs under The Controlled Miss; the zoo example (2515) mentions a third expansion to "anything with a unique shape or quality" that the script never shows; panel placeholders are labeled CH18_ inside Chapter 22; the sentence at 2569 starting "Then have a prepared transition" is grammatically broken.

Ch22 what reads authentically Chris: the "(pun intended)" opener and "do not skip this chapter" (2469); the Invisible Deck breakdown (2474); the zoo and movie False Expansion scripts and the explanation after them (2506-2516); the REFLEX he/she tip including "say 'she' first" (2528-2532); the R.A.I.S.E. anagram wipe-away with the disembodied-spirit script (2541); the Seinfeld/Friends miss line (2570); "that's my favorite type of moment" (2580); "Look here, not there" (2546). Anywhere he names a real effect and walks a real script, the voice is his. Keep those and rebuild the theory paragraphs around them.

Ch23 intro (2604-2609) is the most model-dense stretch in the range: mirrored philosophy/workshop pair, "That distinction matters", "not because you lack methods, but because you lack architecture", table-of-contents signposting (First / Then / Then / Then), "Two is enough.", "The goal isn't X. The goal is Y.", "That one shift changes everything", and a "You're no longer X. You're Y." closer. Nearly every sentence carries a tell. Recommend rewriting the whole intro from scratch in Chris's voice rather than editing sentence by sentence.

Ch23 Stop Using Letters (2612-2618) is mixed: the tiger sensory list (2613) and "handed them a homework problem" (2615) and "If you can find a copy, find it" / "makes the whole thing fly" (2616) are Chris. Fraser Parker is cited without a title while Atlas Brookings gets Train Tracking; mild vague attribution, worth naming the Parker book.

Ch23 Physical Tagging and Multiple/One-Word Titles (2625-2636) are clearly Chris dictating: run-on sentences, double spaces, "You too should utilize", "I will also mention that", "This is a great segue", backticked `fruit to fang`, the Bewitched/Cheers/Frasier walkthrough. Do not humanize these; they are the reference voice for the rest of the chapter. Note the paragraph appears to have a generated summary merged into it ("Physical tagging comes into play once the category exists... They're the most reliable single extraction I know of... Reaction-based pumps come last") and the line "Here is how each one actually works." (2626) lands after the first channel instead of before it.

Tricolon count for the range is about 22, mostly in Ch22 theory sections ("a billet to hand out, a board to write on, a box to seal"; "calibrating, testing, adjusting"; "direction, distraction, and depth"; "Correct. Impressive. Forgettable."; "more interesting than deduction, more flattering than trickery, and more coherent than randomness"). Chris's own lists in dictated passages run to four or five items with no rhythm ("no gimmicks, no props, no pen, no paper"), which is a useful tell for which paragraphs are his.
Em dashes: only one in the range, in the Chapter 22 title line (2466). The prose is already clean of dashes, so the cleanup here is cadence, not punctuation.
group_verdict: Overall this stretch reads like a model that was handed Chris's ideas, with Chris breaking through only where a real effect and a real script appear (Invisible Deck, the zoo and movie expansions, REFLEX he/she, R.A.I.S.E., Seinfeld/Friends, the sitcom arm-grip walkthrough, I Love Lucy vs The Office). The first reader's findings hold up almost entirely; I dropped only three (a content-driven first/second/third rule, a single punch on the end of a dictated paragraph, and a heading em dash that belongs to the build script) and downgraded a handful of mediums to low where a single device sat on otherwise authentic prose. The single most damaging habit is the contrast hammer used as a closer: You're not X. You're Y. / It isn't X. It's Y. / Not X but Y appears roughly thirty times in 175 lines, and because it is the model's default way to end a paragraph, nearly every theory paragraph lands on the same two-beat shape, which flattens Chris's real rhythm (long analytical run, one punch, long again) into punch after punch. The secondary tell that confirms it is machine-made rather than Chris on a roll: the same closer lines were generated more than once (knows/feel the difference even when they can't name it three times, world around the word twice, the two-people-and-an-impossible-thought image four times, the premise-need-not-be-true point three times, the three-failures framing twice), which is what a model does across separate drafts and what a person dictating never does. Rewrite plan for Chris: keep every paragraph that names an effect and walks a script, then rebuild each theory section around those with at most one punch per section, and rewrite the Ch23 intro and the Silence section from scratch rather than sentence by sentence.

chapter_notes: Ch23 Propless Systems (2641-2706): the chapter runs two voices side by side and the seam is usually mid-paragraph. Framework paragraphs (Category Locks opener, Pumps, Build Process intro, the first sentence or two of every Step) carry the model's contrast hammer, fragment stacks, and aphorism closers; the examples Chris dropped in are unmistakably his and should be protected: the 1,500 sitcoms / same fifteen count, the "isn't an ex, is it?" line with the meddling cover, the Dwight / Office reveal script with the hideous yellow shirt, the home-cooked meal vs prepackaged, "Take risks!", "That's no good.", "Go look now. The next sentence is for when you return."

Ch23 negative parallelism: roughly 20 in 60 lines, at least one in every Step (1, 2, 4, 7, 8 open or close on one). "You no longer need X. You need Y" is used twice nine lines apart (2642, 2651). "Matters more than" twice (2665, 2675). "Genuine/genuinely" five times across the range.

Ch23 paragraph endings: every Step section closes on a quotable aphorism (only as strong as the space you build inside of / neighborhood and door / less like luck and more like access / floor and ceiling / true believer, fan, and lifelong contact). Chris's own paragraphs end on an instruction or a shrug ("Try to keep this in mind.", "Use that to your advantage.", "That's no good."). Rewriting even half of these closers into plain instructions would change the feel of the whole chapter.

Ch23 repeated rhetorical move: questions written without question marks in a stack (2683: What is most common in this room. What answer fits the age... ; 2700: Where do you pause. When do you look away.). This is a strong model fingerprint; Chris punctuates questions as questions. Also three noun fragment stacks (Color. Setting. Age. / Fifteen sitcoms. Twelve star-signs. Eight objects. / Category. Emotional quality. Associated image. Specific target.).

Ch23 editing artifacts worth knowing about: "They invent distinctions" at 2675 has no antecedent, and there are double spaces at 2666 ("entire  performance") and 2671 ("A  propless"). These look like hand cuts to a model draft, so the sentences around them are the ones most likely still carrying model cadence.

Ch23 structural: all 8 STEP headings use an em dash (STEP 1 — DEFINE...). Structural, but they violate the standing no-dash rule in public copy; swap to a colon or period in build-book.py. The pull quote "The arc does not exist in the show..." prints twice back to back (2703 and 2706) and does not connect to anything in this chapter; check whether build-book.py is emitting the part divider twice.

Ch24 REFLEX first part (2707-2800): far more Chris than Ch23. The intro hype ("one of my most famous", "maximum of ONE question", "Since this method is ungimmicked, it can work on a video call as well as in person!", "Good news!"), the Timon Krause / Kurotsuke credit, the Mary vs Ava age-name example, the poker chip / straw wrapper / Amazon thumper advice, the Cheat #1 paragraph with its typos ("friend form their childhood"), and "This will take practice! Do not let that stop you." all read hand-written. Leave those alone; a humanizing pass that flattened them would hurt the chapter.

Ch24 where the model shows: the KEY PRINCIPLE boxes and the tell-description paragraphs. Short flat triples ending on a quotable line (2771 limbic system, 2776 photograph vs in person, 2797 no search), the "does two things. It... And it..." enumeration at 2789 (same template as "three jobs" in Ch23), and "It is not a certainty. It is a starting point" at 2759. Negative parallelism is only about 4x here versus about 20x in Ch23. "Make your claim with confidence" appears verbatim at 2736 and 2794.

Ch24 unsourced science: line 2731 asserts fusiform face area, STS, insula, myelination on relevant pathways, and cortical real estate getting redistributed with no citation, immediately next to Chris's gym metaphor that says the same thing plainly. Either cite it or cut to the gym line. Similar but milder at 2797 ("transderivational search"), which is at least a term Chris uses in the Eyes chapter.
Ch24 em dashes: the only two prose em-dash sentences in the whole range are here (2760 and 2797), both bracketing the scripted instruction. Parentheses or a colon fix both.

Ch24 content issue, not voice: line 2772 opens "On the other hand, the thumb will most often sit on the side of the fist" where "On the other hand" is meant literally (the concealing hand) but reads as a transition word, and the next paragraph then describes "the empty hand", so a reader cannot tell which hand 2772 is about. Should say "On the concealing hand".

Stats basis: 5,941 words over 160 lines; 133 non-blank lines of which about 74 are prose paragraphs (the rest are headings, step titles, scripts, the three-item phase list, and image captions). Negative parallelism count is prose only; the two scripted performer lines at 2647-2648 ("You are not thinking of someone you met once. This person mattered.") use the same shape but are the method itself and were not counted or flagged. Em dashes: 16 total, 12 in headings or step titles, 4 in prose.
group_verdict: This stretch is two books stitched together. Ch23 (2641 to 2706) reads mostly model with Chris's examples pasted in: the 1,500 sitcoms count, the "isn't an ex, is it?" line, the Dwight / Office script, the home-cooked meal, "Take risks!", "That's no good," and "Go look now" are unmistakably his, and everything framing them (the Category Locks opener, the Pumps paragraph, the Build Process intro, the first and last sentence of nearly every Step) is the model's. Ch24 (2707 to 2800) flips the ratio: the hype intro, the Timon Krause credit, the Mary vs Ava example, the poker chip and Amazon thumper advice, and the Cheat paragraphs are Chris, and only the tell-description paragraphs and KEY PRINCIPLE boxes carry model cadence. The single most damaging habit is the negative-parallel contrast hammer ("The goal isn't X. The goal is Y," "isn't a weakness, it's good design," "isn't failure, it's your floor," "isn't invisible when X. It's invisible when Y"), which lands roughly twenty times in Ch23's 60 lines, and it is made worse by a second-order pattern the first reader did not name: every Step closes on a quotable aphorism (only as strong as the space, neighborhood and door, luck and access, floor and ceiling, believer fan and lifelong contact) where Chris's own paragraphs close on an instruction or a shrug. Two smaller fingerprints worth a global search: the repeated-word pivot (narrowing reads as narrowing / fishing is visible / compensation is visible / process looks like a process, four times in one chapter) and questions written without question marks in stacks (2683, 2700). Rewriting the Step openers and closers into plain instructions, leaving the examples untouched, would move Ch23 most of the way back to his voice; Ch24 needs only the two em-dash lines, the flat tell paragraphs, and the KEY PRINCIPLE wording.

chapter_notes: Ch24 REFLEX (rest): the cue catalog under More Relevant Cues (2832-2841) is the worst stretch. Ten entries in a row each end on an aphoristic one-liner ("That is the hand." "The search is the signal." "concealment loves volume"), and the identical closer "that is the hand" appears at both 2835 and 2839. The catalog also re-explains the chin tell (2821 vs 2838) and the orientation reflex (2801-2802 vs 2835) in near-duplicate wording, which is elegant-variation behavior rather than Chris repeating himself.

Ch24 REFLEX (rest): punch endings run roughly 27 of about 70 prose paragraphs. Chris's real rate is about one per section. Practicing This Alone (2860-2862) and A Note on Getting It Wrong (2865-2866) close every paragraph on a quotable, three and two in a row respectively.

Ch24 REFLEX (rest): negative parallelism ("not X. It is Y" / "X, not Y") appears about 15 times across the range, with two in the single paragraph at 2801. Em dashes: 34 in 108 lines, clustered in the cue catalog and the IMBALANCED section; a handful are inside scripted lines or letter ranges (K—Z) and are formatting rather than rhetoric.

Ch24 REFLEX (rest): what reads authentically Chris: 2805 (the verbal confirmation paragraph, with "If its a guy", "k-z", "With that said", the run-on explanation and "What to say:" tacked on), 2807 ("This rarely ever happens" and the caps "PIVOT!"), 2814 ("As crazy as this sounds, it is amazingly reliable"), 2828 ("Take credit for the hit!"), 2827's comma-spliced middle, 2845's second half ("You also in the beginning would have instructed them...", "Feel free to use other clever ways"), 2852 (the free web app plug, "Try: ... What is it? Yes, it is Ben.", missing space after "name."), 2855 ("repeat it ploy", numeral "2"), and the backup script at 2856 ("the last 3 times"). These are the voice to rewrite toward; notice they are the passages with typos, numerals, and messy syntax.

Ch24 REFLEX (rest): the IMBALANCED section (2869-2895) is the least Chris-sounding block. It is structured as heading, one-sentence announcement ("Here is the whole engine"), tidy explanation, punch closer, on repeat, and it ends with a generic "Why It Belongs Here" wrap-up. The math paragraphs (2877-2880) are fine and necessary; the framing paragraphs around them (2869, 2883, 2895) are the ones to redo. The Atlas Brookings and Marc Paul credit at 2870 is good and specific; keep it.

Ch24 REFLEX (rest): line 2897 ("You can get a lot of information when you use a which hand as the delivery method.") sits after the section-break glyph and before the PART THREE marker. It sounds like a stray Chris note that never got folded into the chapter. Flagging for placement, not voice.

Ch24 REFLEX (rest): rhetorical-question-then-answer and vague attribution ("research shows") are essentially absent from this range; the machine signal here is almost entirely cadence (contrast hammers, mirrored pairs, staccato closers, em-dash reveals) rather than vocabulary. The only taxonomy vocabulary hits are "Additionally" at 2805 (inside an otherwise authentic paragraph), "genuine" twice (2840, 2841), "dramatically" (2847), and "exactly" (2803, 2895).
group_verdict: Overall this stretch reads like a model with Chris's notes pasted in at intervals. The passages that are clearly him are the messy ones (2805 with "If its a guy" and "k-z", 2807's "PIVOT!", 2814's "As crazy as this sounds", 2820's run-on chin demonstration, 2827's comma-spliced middle, 2828's "Take credit for the hit!", 2845's "Feel free to use other clever ways", 2852's web-app plug and "Yes, it is Ben.", 2856's "the last 3 times" script) and everything around them has been sanded into an even, quotable cadence. The single most damaging habit is the manufactured punchline closer: roughly one aphoristic one-liner per paragraph and one per cue entry ("That is the hand." twice, "The search is the signal." "Anxiety leaks." "All of it is ammunition now." "The deduction becomes a mind-read." "That is the point you are building toward."), where Chris's real rate is about one per section. That habit is what makes the More Relevant Cues catalog (2832-2841), Practicing This Alone (2860-2862), A Note on Getting It Wrong (2864-2866), and the whole IMBALANCED framing (2869, 2883, 2895) sound like the same machine, and it pulls the negative parallelisms and em-dash reveals along with it because they are the setups for those closers. Strip the closers first and most of the other tells lose their reason to exist. I dropped one finding (2847, a plain list of name examples) and downgraded 2816, 2827, and 2802 to low because they are functional stage direction with Chris's own moves in them; everything else holds, and the six missed items are mostly the same closer habit in sentences the first reader referenced but did not quote.

findings.quote: What struck me was not the matrix itself. It was that he could do it anywhere, under any conditions, and blow away magicians who knew the traditional methods, because underneath the routine he had an entire toolkit. Dozens of ways to steal a coin. Dozens of ways to load one.

What got me was that he could do it anywhere, under any conditions, because underneath the routine he had a whole toolkit: a dozen ways to steal a coin, a dozen ways to load one, and every move rehearsed until he did not have to think about it.

It was Y', the 'Dozens... Dozens...' fragment pair, then 'If he made a mistake... If the conditions favored...'. The story would survive with the polish stripped. Medium, not high, because the specifics carry it.

findings.quote: It is not. It is one way, frozen at the moment of publication. The person who created it was never bound by it. Creators carry variations, spare ideas, and outs for every circumstance, because they built the thing and know where it bends.

findings.why: Stacked model cadence: 'It is not. It is Y' contrast hammer, then a tricolon (variations, spare ideas, outs), then a quotable closer ('know where it bends'). Three devices in two sentences.
findings.rewrite: It is not the best way. It is one way, whatever the creator happened to be doing the week they filmed it. The person who built the routine has ten other ways to do every move, because they know where it breaks.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'It is not. It is one way, frozen at the moment of publication' is the contrast hammer, 'variations, spare ideas, and outs' is a tricolon, 'know where it bends' is a manufactured quotable, and the next line (2919) is a one-line paragraph punch on top of it. Four devices in a row.

findings.quote: Mix them. Match them. Add your own. Jam live with a real spectator until you can move between them without thinking, so that whatever a real person throws at you, you have a way through that feels seamless.

findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'Mix them. Match them. Add your own.' is a three-beat imperative fragment stack, and 'seamless' is straight off the vocabulary list. 'Jam live with a real spectator' is Chris; the frame around it is not.

The tell is the closer: 'less like a trick and more like you simply knew' is a contrast formula plus adverb tic tacked on to a table of contents. Downgraded from high to medium.

findings.quote: You watch.

'You watch.' is the only staccato line in the Repeat It Ploy section, and one clipped beat between a script line and the tell instructions is exactly the punch Chris's voice profile allows.
