findings.quote: the details that no public record contains because they live only in the way a person talks about someone they loved
findings.why: Aphoristic clause riding on the same "live" formula as the paragraph's closer, and "each method fills a gap the other leaves open" is a mirror in the sentence before it. Two extra devices in a paragraph the reader flagged only for its chiasmus.
findings.where: Ch28 Digital Pre-show, Combining Standard Pre-show with Digital Pre-show
findings.rewrite: Standard pre-show gives you the stuff no obituary has, like how their voice changes when they talk about the person.

findings.quote: I note my sources, not for any formal reason, but because source awareness matters during delivery.
findings.why: "not for X, but because Y" hammer with an abstract noun ("source awareness") as the reason, inside a first-person paragraph that is otherwise practical. Low on its own, but it is the third contrast construction in three consecutive paragraphs (3716, 3719, 3722).
findings.where: Ch28 Digital Pre-show, The Build: Constructing a Dossier
findings.rewrite: I write down where each thing came from, because how sure I am changes how I say it on stage.

findings.quote: That line, for me, exists clearly.
findings.why: Abstract five-word sentence inside the Chris Michael's Take, wedged between two real story beats. "exists clearly" is model phrasing for a personal rule; Chris would say what the rule is or just move on. Clusters with 3727 and 3730 in the same box.
findings.where: Ch28 Digital Pre-show, Chris Michael's Take
findings.rewrite: I do not say the name of someone who died. That is a hard rule for me.

chapter_notes: Ch28 (rest): the search-string sections (3661 to 3714, Birthdays through Corroboration) are mostly clean. They are instructional, specific, and the operators do the talking. Flags there are light (3684, 3687, 3703, 3709) and mostly rule-of-three list shapes; the literal source lists (Legacy.com, Findagrave, site: operators, the Tools > Any Time > Custom Range instruction) read like Chris and should not be touched.

Ch28 (rest): the model cadence starts at Note on Search History (3716) and gets denser through The Delivery Protocol, The Line, and the Combining section. From 3747 to 3761, almost every paragraph uses the same build: setup sentence, an anaphora run ("You have... You have...", "It tells you... It tells you..."), a contrast hammer ("not X. Y."), and a one-line aphoristic closer. Seven of the last eight paragraphs (3751 to 3761) end on a punch line.

Ch28 (rest): paragraph-ending habits. About 16 of 59 paragraphs end on a quotable closer, and they cluster: 3716 (chiasmus), 3724, 3730, 3736 ("The first acknowledges. The second intrudes."), 3739, 3743 ("invisible by design"), 3753, 3757, 3758 ("where the most powerful mentalism lives"), 3759 ("What you do with the file is the performance"), 3761. One of these per section would be Chris; this is one per paragraph.

Ch28 (rest): negative parallelism appears roughly 18 times in the range, and in 3749 to 3759 it is essentially one per paragraph ("You are not asking for a random name. You are asking...", "This is not meant to be a method. Instead...", "Now you are not performing a name reveal. This has become something more.", "not as information but as impression", "does not function as the reveal. It functions as...", "The name is not the destination. The name is the key...").

Ch28 (rest): repeated aphorism formulas: "X is the Y" (the discipline is documentation; the name is the key; the file is the performance), "where X lives" twice (3672, 3758), "X because X" mirrors (3716, 3739), and two full chiasmus constructions (3716, 3758). These are the same three or four templates recycled.

Ch28 (rest): adverb and intensifier tics: genuine/genuinely four times (3684, 3734, 3750, 3754), "particular weight" and "particular force", "precisely", "deliberately" twice (3749, 3756), "entirely" twice, "quiet" twice (3727, 3754), "crucial" (3756). Also one "in some sense" hedge and one "Perhaps" (3754), the latter reading like Chris's own insertion rather than a model hedge.

Ch28 (rest): anaphora runs occur six times in about 45 prose paragraphs (3709, 3738, 3743, 3750, 3752, 3756) and rhetorical triples about 17 times, though several of those are literal source lists and were not flagged. Only the rhetorical triples (3723, 3730, 3734 x2, 3738, 3745, 3754, 3756, 3757) are flagged.

Ch28 (rest): zero em or en dashes in the range. The dash pass has already been done here; what remains is purely rhythm and rhetoric, so a find-and-replace will not fix it. No vague attribution ("research shows") in this range either; the chapter is method, not science.

Ch28 (rest): what reads authentically Chris and should be protected during rewrite: the greenroom specifics in the Take (iPad in the greenroom, fifty or sixty people, thirty minutes, Chief of Staff, Patricia, forty-two, floral arrangements, going from resistant to open); "I have some notes about this that I will share later on" (3672); "don’t worry" (3716); "For the sake of all of us performers, please handle it accordingly" (3739); "This also allows you to approach topics more sensitively and gauge whether or not they are appropriate before committing it to your show" (3747); "You might not even mention that they have passed... Perhaps you can let the audience tell you this as if you did not know" (3754); "File that." (3750). The tell is that these sentences are looser and slightly clunkier than the polished model paragraphs around them, which is exactly why they sound human. The rewrite should sound more like these and less like the sentences on either side of them.

Ch28 (rest): no contributor-attributed text in this range; everything is in Chris's own voice or the Chris Michael's Take box, so contributor=false throughout. The Part Four divider blurb (3767) and Ch29 hook (3774) are structural; only 3767 was flagged because the "from the arc of an act to the architecture of a career" wording is a taxonomy formula, and the Ch29 hook line reads fine.
group_verdict: The search-string half of this range (3661 to 3714) reads like Chris: operators, site names, the Tools > Any Time > Custom Range instruction, and a loose first-person aside. From the Note on Search History onward the writer changes, and by the Combining section (3747 to 3759) it is almost pure model: nearly every paragraph is built as setup, an anaphora run, a "not X. Y." hammer, and a one-line quotable closer, with the same three or four templates recycled ("X is the Y", "where X lives", A-without-B chiasmus, "the first... the second..."). The Chris Michael's Take is the clearest proof of the split: the greenroom details (iPad, fifty or sixty people, thirty minutes, Patricia, forty-two, floral arrangements) are unmistakably his, and the paragraph that closes it is unmistakably not. The single most damaging habit is the aphoristic paragraph closer stacked one per paragraph, because it turns a practical chapter about how to search and how to pace a reveal into a run of slogans, and it buries the few authentic lines (the "don't worry" aside, "For the sake of all of us performers", "File that.", "Perhaps you can let the audience tell you this") that should be the model for the rewrite. I kept 37 of 39 findings, dropped two (3728 "No names. No specifics." and 3748 "Here is the structure in plain terms.") as Chris's own short-punch and direct-instruction moves used once, and re-graded several downward where the line itself was defensible and only the follow-up paragraph exposed it.

group.label: Ch29 Performance Arc, Ch30 Method Invisibility, Ch31 Patter

findings.quote: Time it. Trust it. Do not explain it. Explanation is the enemy of wonder.
findings.why: Three two-word imperatives in a row, then a quotable aphorism formula (X is the enemy of Y). The next two sentences ("That means your reveals should be easy to understand and follow. They must have clarity.") read like a human patch bolted on after the model punch.
findings.rewrite: Time the reveal, then trust it. Do not explain it afterward. The reveal itself has to be easy to follow, so build the clarity into the reveal, not into a speech about it.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3795. Three two-word imperatives then an X-is-the-enemy-of-Y aphorism, and the two sentences after it ("They must have clarity.") visibly contradict-and-patch the punch. Stages 03, 05, 06 and 07 all carry one of these closers, so it is a stack across the framework, not one punch.

findings.quote: Dopamine peaks during anticipation, not the revelation. Delay the payoff. The delay is what feels good. Trust the discomfort of a room that is holding its breath.
findings.why: Tailing negation, then three short punches in a row. The last two sentences of the paragraph ("for their own comfort", "When done well, this can make one of the biggest differences") sound like Chris; the front half sounds like the model.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3793. Tailing negation then three short verdicts in a row; the back half of the paragraph ("for their own comfort", "When done well") is Chris. Medium because the stage-card format invites terseness.

findings.quote: The last two minutes are not a wind-down. The hippocampus is deciding what to keep from this evening.
findings.why: Contrast hammer plus an abstract brain region as the agent doing the deciding. The long run-on sentence that follows is clearly Chris, which makes the model opener stand out more.
findings.rewrite: Do not treat the last two minutes as a wind-down. That is when the brain is picking what it keeps from tonight.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3797. "not a wind-down" contrast plus hippocampus as the agent, sitting right before an obviously hand-written run-on. It is one device, but it is the fourth stage in a row to open or close on the same shape.

findings.quote: That is the Von Restorff effect — your brain prioritized the visually distinct element. Chapter Three taught you this. The book just demonstrated it.
findings.why: Reveal dash followed by two clipped punch sentences. The self-referential callout is a legitimate device, but the cadence is stock model: statement, dash explanation, mic drop.
findings.rewrite: That is the Von Restorff effect: your brain grabbed the thing that looked different. You read about it in Chapter Three. You just watched it happen.
findings.verifier_reason: Content is at 3811 but the quote will not grep: the file has thin spaces (U+2009) on both sides of the em dash, i.e. effect[U+2009]—[U+2009]your. Cadence call is right: reveal dash, then two clipped mic-drop sentences. The self-demonstrating callout is a good idea; only the rhythm needs Chris.

findings.where: Ch29 Performance Arc, Performance Architecture Framework (Layer Two)
findings.quote: Which effects are sequenced for which people. Where the acquisitional moments sit relative to the revelations. How the emotional arc is designed to build toward the close. Architecture is the plan that exists before you begin.
findings.why: Three subjectless Which/Where/How fragments, then a definitional aphorism as the closer. All four Layer paragraphs (3815-3818) end on the same kind of one-line definition, so the whole framework block has an even, machine-generated rhythm.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3816. Which/Where/How subjectless fragments then a definitional closer, and all four Layer paragraphs (3815 to 3818) end on the same one-line definition.

findings.where: Ch29 Performance Arc, Performance Architecture Framework (Layer Three)
findings.quote: Calibration is what separates a performed sequence from a live performance. The architecture tells you what to do. Calibration tells you when to deviate from it.
findings.why: Mirrored aphorism pair (architecture tells you what, calibration tells you when) stacked on top of an X-separates-Y-from-Z formula. Textbook quotable-closer engineering, and the third punch ending in a row across the Layer paragraphs.
findings.rewrite: Calibration is the live part. The plan says what to do. Calibration is you noticing, mid show, that the plan is wrong for this room and changing it.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3817. "X is what separates Y from Z" plus a mirrored what/when pair is manufactured quotability, and it is the third identical closer in a row in the framework block.

findings.where: Ch29 Performance Arc, Performance Architecture Framework (Layer Four)
findings.quote: Execution is the visible part. It is also the last layer. Everything underneath it determines how well the execution can possibly land.
findings.why: Fourth consecutive Layer paragraph ending on a clipped aphorism. On its own fine; as the fourth in a row it is the model's even cadence.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3818. Plain on its own, but it is the fourth consecutive Layer paragraph ending on a clipped verdict, so the block reads at one even machine tempo.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, epigraph (repeated almost verbatim as the chapter opener at 3834)
findings.quote: The goal is not to hide the method. It is to build a performance the audience cannot trace even while watching.
findings.why: Stock "It is not X. It is Y." and it appears twice within seven lines (3827 epigraph, 3834 opener with "hide things from the audience"). The duplication itself looks like two model drafts that were both kept.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3827 and repeated with synonym swaps at 3834 ("hide things from the audience", "watching everything"). Two near-identical drafts of the same not-X-it-is-Y line seven lines apart is both a cadence tell and a build defect.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, WHAT IT FEELS LIKE
findings.quote: Not because it was fast. Not because you were not paying attention. Because the structure of what you were watching had been built specifically so that looking directly at it would tell you nothing.
findings.why: Not because / Not because / Because. The classic three-beat anaphora with the third beat as the reveal, plus the adverb "specifically" doing inflation work.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3836. Not because / Not because / Because with the third beat as reveal, plus "specifically" as inflation. Textbook.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, WHAT IT FEELS LIKE (paragraph close)
findings.quote: The method was not hidden. It was invisible because the architecture around it made it structurally undetectable. That is not a trick. That is engineering.
findings.why: Two negative parallelisms back to back, "architecture" as the agent, then a That is not X. That is Y. mic drop. Five model devices in four sentences.
findings.rewrite: Nothing was hidden from you. The moment was built so that even staring right at it told you nothing. That is not a trick so much as a build.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3836. Two contrast hammers, "architecture" doing the acting, then "That is not a trick. That is engineering." Probably the single most recognizable model paragraph in Ch30.

findings.quote: Method invisibility is not misdirection. Misdirection asks you to make someone look away. Method invisibility is the art of building a performance in which looking directly at what is happening tells you nothing about how it works. The audience sees everything. The sequence is inexplicable anyway.
findings.why: Definition by negation, "is the art of" aphorism formula, and a two-fragment punch to close. Third negative-parallel paragraph in a row.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3837. Definition by negation, "is the art of" formula, two-fragment punch closer, and it is the third negative-parallel paragraph in a row after the epigraph and 3836.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Separate Method from Payoff
findings.quote: This is the single most important principle in performance invisibility.
findings.why: Superlative inflation. The same move repeats across the range: "most consistently underused" (3845), "most important component" (3887), "most protected moment" (3866), "most important silence" (3943), "most underused calibration tool" (3963), "most reliable authority demonstrations" (3941). Seven "most" claims in 200 lines.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3839. Superlative signpost; I count eight "the most X" claims in the range (3803, 3839, 3845, 3866, 3887, 3941, 3943, 3963), so it is a habit, not a slip.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Separate Method from Payoff
findings.quote: A strong read delivered thirty minutes after it was gathered feels impossible. The same read delivered thirty seconds after it was gathered feels like a trick. The difference is entirely structural.
findings.why: Mirrored A/B sentence pair with a one-line "entirely" verdict. The exact same mirrored pair is re-run at 3849 (thirty seconds vs fifteen minutes), which is the model restating its own point with elegant variation.
findings.rewrite: Give the same read thirty seconds after you got the information and it looks like a trick. Give it thirty minutes later and it looks impossible. Same read. The gap is what changed.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3841. Mirrored thirty-minutes/thirty-seconds pair with an "entirely structural" verdict, and the same pair is re-run at 3845 (performer who / performer who) and 3849. Three restatements of one idea is elegant variation, not emphasis.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Delay Revelation (duplicated verbatim in the Delay Principle box at 3847)
findings.quote: Reveal information gathered in pre-show during the second half of the performance. Separate gathered observations from revelations by at least two other effects.
findings.why: Not a cadence problem, but a build problem: the two sentences appear word for word in the prose (3843) and again in the callout (3847). Reader hits the same text twice in five lines.
findings.verifier_reason: Both sentences appear word for word at 3843 and again inside the Delay Principle box at 3847. Not a cadence problem (pattern label is off) but a real build defect Chris will want to fix, so worth keeping on the list.

findings.quote: The delay is not just a precaution. It is part of what makes the revelation feel impossible. Memory does not preserve a performance the way a video would. It encodes impressions, emotional peaks, and the overall arc.
findings.why: Not-just-X-it-is-Y, then a second negation, then a rule-of-three list. Even, mid-length sentences with no first-person or specific detail.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3848. Not-just / It-is, a second negation, then an impressions/peaks/arc tricolon. No first person, no specifics, even sentence length.

findings.quote: The information is the same. The felt impossibility is categorically different. The audience is not comparing your reveal to the exact sequence of what they observed. They are comparing it to what they remember, and memory has been working in your favor the whole time.
findings.why: Two clipped contrast sentences, "categorically" as inflation, a not X / they are Y pair, and "memory" as the agent working for you as the closer. This is the passage most likely to be read as AI in the chapter.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3849. Two clipped contrasts, "categorically", a not-comparing / they-are-comparing pair, and memory personified as your ally for the closer. Agree this is the passage most likely to be read as AI in the chapter.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Avoid Single-Step Reveals
findings.quote: Single-step reveals make the structure visible. Multi-step reveals make it invisible. A single-step reveal: you observe something, you state it. The audience can draw a straight line. They often do.
findings.why: Mirrored opening pair, colon-definition, then a three-word punch ("They often do."). The next paragraph (3853) ends on "anti-backtracking architecture", and 3855 restates it as "structural protection": same sentence, two synonyms.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3852. Mirrored visible/invisible opener, colon definition, "They often do." punch. The three-way synonym cycling the reader cites (anti-backtracking architecture 3853, structural protection 3855 and 3858) is real.

findings.quote: The acquisition is here. The reveal is there. In between: three distinct moments, each one compelling enough to fully occupy attention. None of them related to the acquisition. The skeptic's rewind hits three walls before they get to the acquisition window.
findings.why: Here/there staccato, colon fragment, subjectless "None of them" fragment. The obstacle-course image and "hits three walls" are good and could be Chris, so this one is a rewrite of rhythm, not idea.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3857. Here/there staccato and subjectless fragments, but the obstacle-course image and "hits three walls" are worth saving. Rewrite of rhythm only.

findings.quote: The proximity is the tell. Spread the distance. Fill it with your best material. The distance is not wasted time. It is structural protection operating exactly as designed.
findings.why: Five short sentences, two imperatives, a not X / It is Y, and "structural protection" for the third time in four paragraphs. The closer sounds like ad copy for a bridge.
findings.rewrite: If the strongest thing you gathered sits right next to the strongest thing you reveal, that closeness is the tell. Put your best material in between. That time is not filler, it is the wall the skeptic has to climb over.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3858. Five short sentences, two imperatives, not-wasted-time / It-is, and "structural protection operating exactly as designed" as the third use of that phrase in four paragraphs.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Wrap Specifics in Human Insight
findings.quote: The language of perception is stronger than the language of knowledge. 'I noticed…' and 'I get the sense…' carry more weight than 'I know…' Certainty sounds like a system. Perception sounds like a human being who sees deeply.
findings.why: "The language of X" formula from the taxonomy, then a mirrored pair (Certainty sounds like / Perception sounds like) ending on "sees deeply". The script examples in between are useful; the framing around them is pure model.
findings.rewrite: Say "I noticed" or "I get the sense" instead of "I know." When you sound certain you sound like a system. When you sound like you are noticing something, you sound like a person who pays attention.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3860. "The language of X" is named in the taxonomy as an aphorism formula, and the Certainty/Perception mirror ending on "sees deeply" is pure model. Keep the two script lines, rewrite everything around them.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Wrap Specifics in Human Insight
findings.quote: The performer who appears to be working to understand is more compelling than the performer who appears to already know. Never name the signal. Name the inference. The audience will fill in the gap with an explanation more generous than the real one.
findings.why: Mirrored "the performer who X / the performer who Y" comparison, then a Never X. Y. contrast hammer. Good advice in model rhythm; one of the more salvageable ones.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3861. Performer-who / performer-who mirror plus "Never name the signal. Name the inference." Direct instruction is Chris's mode, so this one is salvageable with light touch.

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Make Them Remember the Impossibility
findings.quote: The Reveal Ladder is specifically designed to build emotional investment that peaks precisely when the specific is delivered.
findings.why: "specifically", "precisely", and "the specific" in one sentence. Adverb padding that adds emphasis without content.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3864. specifically / precisely / the specific in one sentence. Low on its own, but the adverb tics cluster across the range (deliberately x3, specifically x2, entirely x2, genuine x2, precisely, categorically).

findings.where: Ch30 Method Invisibility, Make Them Remember the Impossibility (chapter close)
findings.quote: After a strong reveal, the audience is feeling. You are not analyzing. Deliver the next beat while they are still in that state. It is the most protected moment in any performance.
findings.why: Feeling / not analyzing contrast plus another "most" superlative closer. Also a likely error: "You are not analyzing" should be "They are not analyzing" given the sentence before it. Chapter ends on a generic closer with no anecdote.
findings.rewrite: Right after a strong reveal the audience is feeling, not thinking. Move to the next beat while they are still there. Nobody is checking your work in that window.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3866. Feeling / not analyzing contrast, superlative closer, and it ends the chapter with no anecdote at all. "You are not analyzing" almost certainly should be "They"; flag for correction either way.

findings.quote: The words are not the performance. The timing between the words is.
findings.why: As an epigraph one contrast line is fine and Chris's follow-up at 3880 ("I want to say that again because I do not think most performers actually believe it") is authentically him. Flagged because 3880 then closes on another mirrored pair: "The silence is where the work happens. The words are just the frame around it."
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3874, but this is a single aphorism in the one slot (an epigraph) where an aphorism belongs, and the paragraph the reader actually objects to (3880) is the most authentically Chris prose in the chapter with one mirrored closer, which is his allowed one punch per section. The cross-chapter epigraph template is better carried by finding 61.

findings.where: Ch31 Patter, WHAT IT FEELS LIKE
findings.quote: You felt the moment arrive before you understood why. And that feeling was not an accident. It was built. Timing is learnable. This is the chapter where you learn it.
findings.why: Not an accident / It was built, then two more clipped punches and a signpost closer. Five sentences, all under nine words, all landing like closers.
findings.rewrite: You felt the moment arrive before you knew why. That was not luck. Somebody built it, and you can learn to build it too. That is what this chapter is for.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3882. Not an accident / It was built, then "Timing is learnable. This is the chapter where you learn it." Five closers in a row.

findings.quote: No breath. No architecture. No sense that the performer knows which moments are load-bearing and which ones are connective tissue.
findings.why: No / No / No triple fragment with "architecture", "load-bearing", and "connective tissue" packed into one line. "I have seen this over and over" just before it is Chris; this is not.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3883. No / No / No anaphora with architecture, load-bearing and connective tissue all in one line, immediately after an authentic "I have seen this over and over."

findings.quote: Almost every performer rushes the reveal. Not dramatically. Just by one beat. They get to the moment, feel the tension, and resolve it slightly faster than they should. The reason is physical. Tension is uncomfortable. The body wants to discharge it. You have to override that instinct deliberately.
findings.why: Not dramatically / Just by one beat fragments, a tricolon, then four staccato sentences ending on "deliberately". Every sentence is a verdict.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3886. Eight sentences, every one a verdict, two fragments, a tricolon, and a "deliberately" closer. The observation itself (one beat early, body wants to discharge) is good and survives a rewrite.

findings.quote: The deceleration is the reveal's most important component. More important than the words. More important than the final line.
findings.why: Superlative, then two "More important than" fragments. Paragraph closes on the mirrored punch "If you rush, you arrive before they do." The concrete drill in 3888 (ten seconds, thirty percent) is the human part; keep that, cut this.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3887. Superlative, two "More important than" fragments, and "If you rush, you arrive before they do." as the mirrored closer. The 3888 drill with ten seconds and thirty percent is the human part.

findings.quote: You are not manufacturing drama. You are giving the room time to catch up with what they already sense is coming. They know something is about to happen. Give them the space to feel it before you confirm it.
findings.why: You are not X / You are Y followed by two punch lines. The first half of the paragraph is a real drill; the back half is the model explaining the drill's meaning.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3888. Not manufacturing / You are giving, then two punch lines explaining the drill. Front half of the paragraph stays.

findings.where: Ch31 Patter, After a Statement Lands
findings.quote: That second is not wasted time. It is the moment where the experience becomes real for the audience, not just the participant.
findings.why: Not wasted time / It is the moment (same construction as 3858), with a tailing not-just. "I think of this as letting the echo happen" earlier in the paragraph is Chris and worth keeping.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3890. It is one contrast at the end of a section that contains "I think of this as letting the echo happen", so by the density rule it is close to Chris's allowance. Kept low only because "not wasted time. It is the moment" is the identical construction to 3858.

findings.quote: If you accelerate slightly — moving into the next moment with the same or more energy than before — you communicate that what just happened was not a problem. It was texture.
findings.why: Paired em dashes, negative parallelism, and a one-word aphoristic closer ("texture"). Three of the biggest tells in one sentence. The paragraph opened with "That instinct is wrong." as its own punch.
findings.rewrite: If you pick the energy up a notch going into the next moment, the room reads it as: that was nothing. It gets filed as part of the show, not a mistake.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim at 3893. Paired em dashes, not-a-problem / It-was-texture, one-word closer, after a "That instinct is wrong." punch opener. One of only two prose em-dash sentences in the range and both are the reveal-dash shape.

findings.quote: This is the oldest principle in mentalism and the most consistently underused. The performer who delivers a strong read fifteen minutes after establishing it gets a different reaction than the performer who delivers it immediately.

Adds stage 03 to the stage-closer pattern the finder found in 05, 06 and 07.

chapter_notes: Ch29 Performance Arc (3779-3820): Mostly reads human. The seven stage descriptions have run-ons, comma splices and practical hedges ("which can be used to your advantage", "Things can go wrong without you losing the slightest bit of composure", the long EMBED sentence) that are clearly Chris editing over a template. The checklist is structural and fine. "If it looks pristine after six months, you are not using it" is authentic. The model surfaces in two places: the stage closers ("Time it. Trust it. Do not explain it.", "The delay is what feels good.") and the four-Layer Performance Architecture Framework block at 3815-3818, where every paragraph ends on a definitional aphorism and 3817 is a full chiasmus. Em dashes here are all in headings or the callout.

Ch30 Method Invisibility (3824-3866): The most uniformly machine-cadenced chapter in the range. Zero first-person, zero venue/name/number anecdotes, and every section closes on a one-line verdict (I counted 20 punch endings in 43 lines). Negative parallelism appears 13 times; the "is not X. It is Y." shape opens the epigraph, the chapter, and four of the six sections. The same idea is restated with elegant variation three separate times: thirty-minutes-vs-thirty-seconds (3841 and 3849), "anti-backtracking architecture" vs "structural protection" (3853, 3855, 3858), and the Delay Principle text duplicated verbatim between prose and callout (3843, 3847). Also the epigraph is duplicated as the opener (3827, 3834). "Structural/structure/architecture" appears 20 times across the range, most of it here. Two likely defects to fix regardless of voice: "You are not analyzing" at 3866 should read "They", and the duplicate callout text. Nothing in this chapter reads as Chris; the ideas are his, the sentences are not.

Ch31 Patter, Rhythm, and Silence (3871-3972): Split personality. The semantic satiation section (3917-3936) is the most authentically Chris prose in the whole range: the door exercise with finger counting, "If English is not your first language... That matters.", "if you are a magician and a carpenter, then welcome back, Jesus. Glad you are reading my book", the odd "to make sure no regrets are made" phrasing, the A/B post test instructions, and the five-websites-in-a-row observation. Keep all of that. But the science paragraphs inside it (3925, 3927, 3928) revert to model mode with three tricolons per paragraph, not-just-but, and "The real lesson". The pacing sections (3884-3894, 3937-3965) are dense model cadence: negative parallelism appears roughly 33 times in this chapter alone, "does two things / does three things" signposting twice, and nearly every paragraph ends on a punch (I counted about 32). The Recovery Protocol levels each close on an identical "X, not Y" tail. Silence gets the same "is not X. It is Y." treatment three times (3874, 3946, 3947). The four prose em dashes in the range all live here (3893, 3941), and both are the paired reveal-dash pattern. Superlative inflation ("most important", "most underused", "most reliable", "most protected") appears seven times across the range, five of them in this chapter. Chris Michael's Take at 3971 has a real anecdote (400-person gala, wrong matrix row) wrapped in model one-liners; the story can stay, the wrapper needs his phrasing. Editing bug: 3939 opens with "They" and has no antecedent.

Cross-range vocabulary: no classic AI nouns (delve, tapestry, landscape, leverage) appear; the tells are all rhythm. Adverb/inflation tics: deliberately x3, specifically x2, entirely x2, genuine x2, precisely, categorically. Abstract agents recur: memory "working in your favor", the hippocampus "deciding", the nervous system "treating", architecture "making it undetectable". Every chapter epigraph in range (Ch30, Ch31, Ch32) uses the not-X-it-is-Y template, which will read as a house style the model imposed rather than a choice Chris made.
group_verdict: Taken as a whole this stretch reads like a model with Chris's ideas loaded into it, with three genuine exceptions: the hand-edited stage cards and checklist in Ch29, the 3880 "I want to say that again" paragraph, and the semantic satiation section (door drill, the Jesus joke, the A/B post test, the five-websites observation), which is the only place in 200 lines with first person, a joke, a number, and a mess. Everything else, including all of Ch30 and the pacing sections of Ch31, is uniform in rhythm and has zero venues, names, or field anecdotes until the 400-person gala in Chris Michael's Take. The single most damaging habit is the negative-parallelism closer, the "X is not Y. It is Z." shape: it opens all three chapter epigraphs, opens Ch30 twice, and ends nearly every paragraph in Ch30 and the Ch31 pacing sections (roughly 7 in 43 lines of Ch30, 15 or more in Ch31 by a narrow count, plus the four identical "X, not Y" tails on the Recovery Protocol levels). Because it lands as a verdict every time, it flattens the long-paragraph-then-punch rhythm that is actually his into punch, punch, punch, and once a reader notices it they stop hearing Chris. Fixing that one habit, and cutting the three synonym-cycled restatements in Ch30 (thirty seconds versus later, anti-backtracking architecture versus structural protection, the duplicated Delay Principle text), would recover more of his voice than any vocabulary pass.

findings.quote: It was neither. It was a cascade event — initiated at a specific moment, with a specific person, under specific conditions. A standing ovation is not the audience’s decision. It is the performer’s design. This chapter is that design.

findings.verifier_reason: Verified. Four abstract-noun-plus-verb fragments then the 'construct / maintain' mirror, immediately after the authentic 'I almost did not include this topic in the book.' The voice switch is audible mid-paragraph.

findings.rewrite: The rule: never escalate intimacy faster than rapport can justify. That means no strong eye contact plus lingering touch before they feel safe, no walking into a closed body, and no making the participant deal with your need for connection in front of the room.
findings.verifier_reason: Verified, downgraded. Four 'Do not' sentences in a paragraph labeled 'The practical rule', so imperatives are expected; Chris does give rules directly. The liturgy shape is the tell, not the content. Medium.

findings.why: 'It is not. It is...' hinge into a tricolon of paired abstractions. Opens the section's closing paragraph.

findings.quote: The pre-show checklist is not about eliminating uncertainty. Uncertainty is part of the work. It is about eliminating the preventable failures — the logistics that surface mid-show, the volunteer who was never profiled, the introduction that handed the room to you facing the wrong direction.
findings.why: The reader quoted only the last two sentences of this paragraph. The front half is the bigger offender: 'not about X. It is about Y', anadiplosis on 'uncertainty. Uncertainty', and an em-dash tricolon of failures, all before the 'variable' closer.
findings.rewrite: The checklist will not remove uncertainty. Uncertainty is the job. What it removes is the stuff you could have prevented: the AV problem that shows up mid-show, the volunteer you never profiled, the intro that handed you a room facing the wrong way.

findings.quote: The best show you can give happens before the lights come up. Every item on this list addresses a variable that, if left unmanaged, will surface during the performance at a cost that is always higher than the cost of handling it in advance.
findings.why: Mentioned in the reader's why for 4128 but never quoted. Aphorism opener, 'variable' again, and a cost/cost mirror that inflates a plain point (do prep early). With 4128 it forms a two-paragraph model preamble to a list.
findings.rewrite: Most of the show happens before the lights come up. Everything on this list is something that will bite you mid-show if you leave it alone, and it is always cheaper to handle it the day before.

findings.quote: Most performers who trigger this reaction are not trying to be creepy. They are usually just moving too fast, too close, or too intensely for the level of rapport they have earned. The reason it happens so quickly is biological.
findings.why: Not flagged at all. 'not trying to X. They are usually just Y' hinge, a tricolon of 'too', a 'The reason is [one word]' punch, and the paragraph then closes on 'stops engaging wonder and starts engaging threat-monitoring', a stops/starts mirror of two abstractions. Four model moves in one paragraph.
findings.rewrite: Most performers who get this reaction are not trying to be creepy. They are moving faster, closer, or more intensely than the rapport they have actually earned, and the body clocks that mismatch in a fraction of a second.

findings.quote: These are two separate design decisions. The peak should be the most emotionally intense moment of the show. The close should be the most meaningful. They are rarely the same moment, and conflating them is a structural mistake.
findings.why: The reader's chapter note says Peak vs. Close is four consecutive paragraphs each closing on a mirror, but only quoted 3996, 3997, 3998. This is the missing first one: 'The peak should be... The close should be...' mirrored pair with a 'structural mistake' tag.
findings.rewrite: The peak and the close are two different decisions. The peak is the most intense moment in the show. The close is the most meaningful one. They are almost never the same moment, and if you try to make them the same moment you lose one of them.

findings.why: Listed in the reader's notes as one of the four 'not only' hinges but never quoted as a finding. 'not only X. They are Y' into an abstract closer ('the emotional freedom of the moment'), in the section that runs 4060, 4064, 4065, 4066 back to back.
findings.rewrite: They are not just reacting to the effect. They are reacting with the guy who built the moment standing two feet away watching them, and that changes how free they feel to react at all.

findings.quote: A group warms up faster when it feels like you are actually with them, rather than simply performing at them.
findings.why: Preposition-swap aphorism ('with them / at them'), the same device as 'to them / through them' at 4157. A recurring model trick the reader caught once and missed here; it closes the Get Their Names section, whose other two paragraphs also end on tags.
findings.rewrite: A group warms up faster when they can tell you actually care who they are.

chapter_notes: Ch32 When the Room Rises (3984-4011). Attribution is clean: Mann/Uppsala and Kahneman/Fredrickson are named, no 'research shows'. What reads as Chris: the caps 'FORCED' in the deck line, the 'I have seen this from the stage' paragraph with its parenthetical '(usually front left, usually someone who was leaning forward for the last ten minutes)', and above all the Song Anchor paragraph at 4000, which is unmistakably hand-written (run-on syntax, 'by the end' twice, 'If that line is used cleverly'); the hand additions at 4008-4009 ('You may also consider leaving something unresolved', 'it's always stronger when they are not told') are also his. Do not polish those into the model's register; the register jump between 4000 and 4002 is itself the loudest tell in the chapter. Problems: 'It is not X. It is Y.' appears 6 times in about 1,000 words; every section except Song Anchor ends on a mirrored two-beat aphorism (3991, 3993, 3996, 3997, 3998, 4010); Peak vs. Close is four consecutive paragraphs each closing on a chiasmus; the chapter is bookended with 'This chapter is that design', a template reused verbatim in shape at 4124.

Ch33 The Art of Strolling (4012-4108). Two halves with visibly different provenance. First half (4025-4053) is the 90-second-set catalog: every subsection ends on an aphorism (4028, 4034, 4037, 4045, 4049, 4053) and 'is not X. It is Y' hits in four consecutive subsections. Second half (4055-4107) carries the real Chris material: 'Marcus Eddie taught me this', the actual scripts ('My name is Chris Michael. Thank you so much for having me over here', 'decide which one of you is the most unpredictable person in this group', 'Give them a hand so the other tables know you had a good time'), the corporate-host walk-over, and the compliment lines. Keep every script and name. The connective prose between them is the model: ten single-sentence paragraphs used as punches (4064, 4069, 4071, 4084, 4095, 4098, 4102, 4103, 4105, 4106); 'not only X. It is also Y' 4x (4055, 4063, 4089, 4107); 'You are no longer X. You are Y' 3x (4080, 4085, 4087); tricolons about 15x in this chapter, of which the five worst are quoted; 'One of the most [superlative]' or 'An underused' section openers 5x (4030, 4068, 4073, 4094, 4171 in Ch34). Everything is 'the strongest', 'the most reliable', 'the most powerful'. 'Emotional weather' (4056) is later recycled as 'social weather' (4155). Choose the Right Volunteer (4102-4107) is the densest cluster in the whole range: five mirrored one-liners back to back.

Ch34 Making the Room Say Yes (4109-4188). The chapter thesis is stated four times in nearly identical 'Compliance is not X. It is Y' form (4115 epigraph, 4124, 4147, 4160); keep one, cut three. The Pre-Show Master Checklist (4129-4143) is structural and mostly fine as list copy; its framing paragraphs (4127, 4128, 4144, 4145) are pure model and should be rewritten or cut. 'Variable' is the model's closer noun 3x (4085, 4145, 4152). 'genuine/genuinely' 9x across the range, five of them in this chapter. Em dashes: 23 in range (15 in prose, 5 in the 'Seconds 0–10' style subheadings which also carry 4 en dashes, 3 in chapter-title lines); the prose ones are mostly the 'X — Y' reveal or a dashed tricolon aside (4132, 4152, 4170). Mirror Neurons section: 'Instruction tells. Modeling activates.' is model cadence, and the claim itself is stated harder than the human evidence supports (worth a look against the book's evidence tiers; 'people copy what they see' is the safer and more Chris way to say it). Creepy Collapses the Frame opens authentically ('I almost did not include this topic in the book') and contains real behavioral content (ventral side, insula/dACC, the touch-plus-eye-contact mistake, the needy over-asking observation) but every paragraph closes on a mirror or a four-fragment stack, and 4175 is a four-line 'Do not' liturgy. What reads as Chris here: the after-dinner crowd 'whose energy peaked with dessert', the phone-checking tell, 'They spent money to have you there', and the honest admission that performers never get feedback about creepiness.

Range-wide rhythm note: the overriding tell is not vocabulary (AI-word hits are light: 'high-leverage' 2x, 'significantly' 1x, 'architecture' 10x as the chapter's pet abstraction) but paragraph shape. Across 119 prose paragraphs, roughly 60 end on a one- or two-line aphoristic punch and roughly 57 negative-parallelism hinges appear, about one every 110 words. Chris's own voice profile allows one punch per section; here it is one per paragraph, often two. The fix is mostly subtraction: keep the first punch in each section, convert the rest back into ordinary sentences with a 'because' or a concrete example, and let the real scripts, names, and field details (Marcus Eddie, front-left starter, dessert crowd, the two-minute return) carry the authority they already have.
group_verdict: This stretch reads like a model that was handed Chris's notes. The real Chris is easy to find and it is the best material here: the front-left starter who has been leaning forward for ten minutes, the hand-typed Song Anchor paragraph at 4000, 'Marcus Eddie taught me this', the actual table scripts ('decide which one of you is the most unpredictable person in this group', 'Give them a hand so the other tables know you had a good time'), the corporate host walk-over, the after-dinner crowd whose energy peaked with dessert, and 'I almost did not include this topic in the book'. Everything connecting those pieces is the model, and the single most damaging habit is the 'It is not X. It is Y.' hinge used as the default way to close a paragraph. It appears roughly once every hundred words across all three chapters, it opens Ch32 and Ch34 with the identical 'This chapter is that design / how it works' template, it restates the Ch34 thesis four times, and in Ch33's second half it stacks into runs of five mirrored one-line paragraphs (4102 to 4106). Because every paragraph lands on a slide-worthy contrast, the reader stops hearing a performer explain something at a table and starts hearing a deck. Everything else the first reader catalogued (tricolons, 'no longer X', 'variable', 'architecture', the 'One of the most' section openers) is downstream of that one reflex. The fix is subtraction: keep one punch per section, turn the rest back into ordinary sentences with a 'because' or a concrete example, and let the scripts and field details carry the authority they already have. The first reader's list is accurate (every quote verified), slightly over-graded in the checklist and intro-blurb areas, and thin on Ch34's framing paragraphs, which are added above.

findings.quote: The live host introduction is the single most unreliable variable in a corporate performance. Solve it.
findings.why: Epigraph sentence is then repeated word for word inside the body paragraph at 4203, and the two-word command closer is the model's imperative punch. One of the two copies should go.
findings.verifier_reason: Quote is verbatim and the lede really is repeated word for word inside 4203. A standfirst is a structural slot, and a two-word command is inside Chris's range (Give him 50%), so the cadence itself is a tic, not a fingerprint. The actionable note is the duplication: cut one copy.

findings.quote: it establishes the specific credibility most relevant to this audience, it creates genuine anticipation, and it arrives in the client's language, referencing their company, their event, their people, rather than in generic performer biography language.
findings.why: Anaphoric it/it/it list plus an inner their/their/their triple plus 'genuine' plus a tailing 'rather than' contrast, all in one sentence. Stacked devices, not a person explaining a video.
findings.rewrite: It plays before you walk in, it tells the room why you matter to them specifically, and it says their company name out loud. That last part alone is worth the production cost.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Four-item it/it/it/it anaphora with an inner their/their/their triple, 'genuine anticipation', and a tailing 'rather than' contrast, following 'solves this problem entirely'. That is a stacked-device sentence, and the paragraph around it (4203) is the most human moment in the range, which makes the drop-off obvious.

findings.quote: That sentence does not require the room to translate your experience into their context. It arrives already translated.
findings.why: 'Does not X. It Y.' with a mirrored verb (translate / translated) as a quotable closer. Same gloss template ('X means Y. Not A. Something like: B. [punch]') is used for every checklist item that follows.
findings.rewrite: Skip the Fortune 500 line. For a financial services crowd say something like: has worked with leadership at Bloomberg and Deloitte on how behavioral science shows up in a high stakes negotiation. Now nobody in the room has to translate you.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'Does not X. It Y.' with the mirrored translate/translated is a quotable closer the model builds. The template claim holds: 4207 ends on 'The window closes.', 4209 on the anticipation chain, 4210 on 'Say their name. Reference the event.', 4211 on 'already waiting for it.' Every checklist gloss lands the same way.

findings.quote: The brain immediately begins generating questions. Those questions are anticipation. Anticipation is the compliance runway you need before you enter.
findings.why: Chain aphorism (questions are anticipation, anticipation is the runway) with abstract nouns doing the acting and an 'X is the Y of Z' formula closer. Preceded by another 'Not X. Instead: Y' in the same paragraph.
findings.rewrite: Say what they are about to see, not what you do. Something like: in a few minutes you are going to watch a guy tell a total stranger in this room something he could not possibly know. Now the room has questions, and a room with questions is waiting for you.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. Anadiplosis chain (questions... Those questions are anticipation. Anticipation is...) ending on an 'X is the Y' aphorism formula, with 'Not "Chris will perform mentalism." Instead:' earlier in the same paragraph. Nobody talks in this chain.

findings.quote: The video ends. There is a beat of silence. Then you enter. That silence is part of the design. Do not fill it.
findings.why: Five clipped sentences in a row with a two-beat command ending. As a callout box it is borderline, but the next paragraph repeats the same three beats in prose, so the staccato is doing nothing the prose does not.
findings.where: Ch35 The Intro Video (Timing Note box)
findings.verifier_reason: This is the Timing Note callout box. The wording is a plain three-step sequence plus an instruction ('Do not fill it'), which is what a callout box is for and is inside Chris's short-instruction register. The real issue is the body text underneath restating it in staccato, and findings 5 and 6 already cover that body text.

findings.quote: You are not waiting for the AV technician to catch up. You are holding the space so the audience feels the transition.
findings.why: 'You are not X. You are Y.' contrast hammer, stacked directly after 'It is the equivalent of the pause before a strong line' and directly before the operational versus intentional dash line at 4215.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'You are not X. You are Y.' sits in a paragraph that also has 'is doing specific work', 'installed an authority frame', and 'the equivalent of the pause before a strong line'. Cluster holds.

findings.quote: That distinction — operational versus intentional — is felt by the room before you say anything.
findings.why: Paired em dashes bracketing a coined antithesis, passive 'is felt by the room', and a 'before you say anything' punch. Also preceded by 'You chose this moment to arrive', a manufactured one-liner.
findings.rewrite: Come in too fast and it looks like you are just next on the run sheet. Hold the beat and it looks like you picked the moment. The room feels that before you open your mouth.
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim, both em dashes present. Paired dashes bracketing a coined antithesis, passive 'is felt by the room', preceded by the manufactured one-liner 'You chose this moment to arrive.' Nothing in Chris's corpus uses dash brackets; his asides are parentheses and ellipses.

findings.quote: The five minutes before you enter the room are not dead time. They are the last window you have to manage your own state, confirm the operational details, and set the conditions for a clean entry.
findings.why: 'Are not X. They are Y' followed by a rule-of-three, then the paragraph closes with a subjectless fragment ('Hesitation that the audience will read and interpret, accurately, as something being slightly wrong').
findings.verifier_reason: Verbatim. 'Are not dead time. They are the last window' plus a tricolon, and the paragraph closes on a subjectless fragment with an interrupting 'accurately,' which is a very model-shaped sentence.
